articles.title: How to Compare VPS Deals Beyond the Headline Price
articles.description: A practical way to compare VPS deals by workload fit, renewal terms, management, backups, bandwidth, and the work you will own.
articles.question: How do I compare VPS deals when providers bundle different resources, billing terms, and support?
articles.body:
If two VPS deals advertise different bundles, compare the server you can actually run and the recurring obligations you accept—not the headline alone. Match CPU, memory, storage, and network terms to your workload; then check renewal billing, paid add-ons, management responsibility, backup and restore options, and region. Put unknown terms in an “unverified” column instead of assuming they are included.

## Start with the workload, not the plan label

“VPS” does not describe one standard bundle. A plan name or a large storage figure cannot tell you whether a server fits your application. Write down what the workload needs: operating system, memory headroom, CPU behavior, persistent disk, outbound transfer, and the location that makes sense for your users. Then match each need to a published plan field. If a provider does not disclose a field, mark it unknown and decide whether you can accept that uncertainty.

This is a comparison method, not a benchmark claim. The useful question is not “Which card looks bigger?” but “Which listed resource could become the first constraint for my workload?” For a database, memory and storage behavior may deserve closer review; for a file or media service, outbound transfer may matter more. Those are workload-based priorities, not promises about a provider’s performance.

[DigitalOcean’s Droplet creation documentation](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/how-to/create/) shows why labels alone are insufficient: its creation flow separates configuration choices such as region, image, CPU, memory, storage, backup, and networking. Its [Droplet pricing documentation](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/pricing/) also distinguishes plan types and explains that billing behavior depends on the selected configuration. Read the plan’s own details rather than transferring assumptions from another provider.

## Compare the bill across the same time horizon

A promotional headline and the amount due later answer different questions. For each candidate, record the initial billing term, what the next renewal uses, whether billing is recurring automatically, and which extras are selected or required. Compare the same period for every plan. If one quote is for a short initial term and another reflects continuing service, they are not yet comparable.

Use this worksheet:

- Base service for the chosen billing term
- Required management or control-panel options
- Backup, snapshot, or additional storage options
- Usage charges, including outbound transfer where applicable
- Renewal terms and automatic-renewal behavior
- Taxes or checkout fees shown before payment

The comparison formula is: **cost for the chosen period = base service + required add-ons + usage-based charges + applicable taxes and fees.** This is a worksheet, not a quote; fill it only from the current plan page and checkout. Do not treat a missing line item as free.

Billing details are provider-specific. [Namecheap documents hosting invoice and renewal timing](https://www.namecheap.com/support/knowledgebase/article.aspx/10567/21/hosting-packages-life-cycle/) and how renewal dates relate to the selected billing cycle. [DigitalOcean documents different Droplet billing models](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/pricing/), including the fact that some plans continue billing while powered off. The practical lesson is to look for the event that ends billing and the term used for renewal; do not assume “stop” or “cancel” means the same thing across services.

## Price the work you would otherwise do yourself

Management changes what a low headline buys you. Before comparing plans, answer plainly: who installs and updates core software, who investigates a service failure, who handles recovery, and who has administrator access? [Namecheap documents distinct VPS management modes](https://www.namecheap.com/support/knowledgebase/article.aspx/9304/48/what-vps-management-options-do-you-provide/), with different responsibilities and access levels. [Liquid Web’s package page](https://www.liquidweb.com/vps-hosting/packages/) presents managed infrastructure and backups as included package features. These are examples of different bundles, not a universal ranking.

Translate that difference into work, not a made-up dollar amount. If you choose a user-managed server, list the maintenance tasks you are ready to own. If you choose a managed bundle, confirm exactly which services are included and which remain your responsibility. A bundle that removes work can be the better fit for an operator who cannot maintain the server; the same bundle may be unnecessary for someone who wants full control and already handles operations.

## Treat backup words as separate promises

“Backup included” is not a complete recovery plan. Check whether the offer means automatic backups, on-demand snapshots, or both; where copies are stored; how often they are created; how long they are retained; and whether restoring is self-service. Also ask whether backup storage is included or separately billed.

[Namecheap’s VPS backup guide](https://www.namecheap.com/support/knowledgebase/article.aspx/10085/2188/how-to-set-up-automated-backups-for-vps-and-dedicated-server/) describes configurable backup types, schedules, and retention controls, including the risk of storing copies on the same server. [DigitalOcean describes backups and snapshots](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/how-to/create/) as different options, with backups enabled separately in its create flow and snapshots created on demand. Those details show why a provider’s feature label is only the start of the check. Decide what loss window your workload can tolerate, then verify that the documented recovery option meets it. If you cannot find a restore procedure, count recovery as unverified.

## Check network and location terms

Record the region offered for the plan and whether it serves the people or systems that will use it. Then look for the included transfer allowance, how usage is measured, whether inbound and outbound traffic are treated differently, and whether usage is pooled across servers. [DigitalOcean’s billing documentation](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/pricing/), for example, describes outbound transfer allowances and team-level pooling. That is a provider-specific billing rule; another host may define transfer differently.

Do not compare “bandwidth” labels until you know what each one measures. A port speed, a transfer allowance, and a traffic policy are different fields. If a plan page uses one word without defining it, ask support or leave it marked unknown rather than turning the label into a performance promise.

## A quick decision rule before checkout

Make one row per candidate with five columns: workload fit, continuing bill, management tasks, recovery path, and network or region limits. Mark each item **verified**, **unknown**, or **does not fit**. This simple status system prevents a polished offer card from hiding a missing term.

Imagine one plan has a lower headline but leaves software maintenance and backups to you, while another groups operational help into its package. Neither wins by definition. If you can do the maintenance and have an independent backup process, the first may suit your operating model. If you need the provider to handle specified tasks, compare the second’s written scope with your actual needs. This is a hypothetical comparison, not a claim about a current offer.

Choose a VPS deal only after the checkout page agrees with your worksheet. Keep a copy of the plan terms, renewal setting, and selected options. If a field changes between the plan card and checkout, use the checkout terms for the decision and verify the discrepancy with the provider before paying. The “best deal” is the offer whose published resources, total obligations, and recovery path fit your use—not simply the one with the most attractive first line.

articles.title: How Much Notice Do You Need to Cancel a VPS Deal? The Auto-Renewal Switch, Priced
articles.description: Three providers, three different answers, and only one of them is literally 'cancel anytime'. Read on 2026-10-12: DigitalOcean needs zero notice but makes committed spend non-cancelable, Hostinger's auto-renewal is on by default and can charge up to 30 days before your term ends, and Hetzner requires 30 days' notice to the end of a calendar month.
articles.question: Does cancelling a VPS require advance notice, and is auto-renewal switched on by default?
articles.body:
**The short answer, read off the providers' own legal pages on 2026-10-12: there is no industry-wide notice period, and the phrase "cancel anytime" is doing work it does not deserve.** DigitalOcean genuinely needs zero notice. Hostinger also says "Cancel anytime" — but its Terms of Service say the renewal is charged *"from 30 (thirty) to 0 (zero) calendar days before the end of the current subscription period"*, so on a 24-month plan your real deadline is **month 23 of 24**, not month 24. Hetzner is the only one of the three with an actual contractual notice period: **30 days, to the end of a calendar month**.

And the switch itself is not a switch everywhere. DigitalOcean has no auto-renewal toggle to find, because it does not sell subscriptions — it bills usage in arrears on the first of each month. Hostinger's toggle exists and is **on by default**. Hetzner's contract simply *"continue[s] and automatically renew[s] [itself] until terminated by either party"*.

| Provider | Notice you must give | Auto-renewal mechanism | Source read 2026-10-12 |
|---|---|---|---|
| DigitalOcean | **0 days** — cancel anytime via account settings or support | No toggle; usage invoiced in arrears on the 1st | ToS §6.3 (Last Updated 22 Aug 2026) |
| Hostinger | **0 days to flip the toggle, but it must land before the Charge Date — up to 30 days before term end** | Toggle exists, **default ON** | ToS §16 (Last revised 2026-09-29 14:31:57) |
| Hetzner | **30 days, to the end of a calendar month** | No toggle; contract auto-renews until terminated | General T&C §2.6 (v2.0.0, 27 Oct 2021); US Special Terms §7 |
| Liquid Web | Not verifiable (403 to direct request) | Not verifiable | — |
| Namecheap | Not verifiable (403 to direct request) | Not verifiable | — |

## The Hostinger number nobody puts on the deal page

Hostinger's VPS page is the most honest of the three about the renewal price and the most misleading about the cancellation. Every one of its four KVM cards prints this line directly above the buy button, read on 2026-10-12:

> Choose plan **Renews at $11.99/mo for 2 years. Cancel anytime.**

Two sentences, and the second one quietly contradicts the Terms of Service the first one depends on. Here is the card data and what it costs over a full 24-month term:

| Plan | List price (struck) | Promo /mo | Renewal /mo | Renewal increase | Promo, 24 mo | Renewal, 24 mo |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KVM 1 | $19.49 | $6.49 | $11.99 | **+84.7%** | $155.76 | **$287.76** |
| KVM 2 | $24.49 | $8.99 | $14.99 | **+66.7%** | $215.76 | **$359.76** |
| KVM 4 | $42.99 | $12.99 | $28.99 | **+123.2%** | $311.76 | **$695.76** |
| KVM 8 | $73.99 | $25.99 | $49.99 | **+92.4%** | $623.76 | **$1,199.76** |

Now the part that changes how you read the whole deal. Hostinger's ToS §16 states that auto-renewal renews *"for a subsequent subscription period, the length of which is equal to the most recent subscription period before renewal or the initial subscription period"*. The period you bought was **2 years**. So the renewal is not a $11.99 charge — it is **one charge of $287.76**, because `11.99 × 24 = 287.76`. Across all four plans the renewal term is **$2,543.04 against a promo term of $1,307.04, a $1,236.00 swing**, and it lands as four single transactions, not 48 monthly ones.

The formula, so you can run it on any card:

```
renewal lump sum = (renewal $/mo) × (months in the term you originally bought)
effective cancellation deadline = term end date − up to 30 days
```

### The "67% off" badge and the renewal price use different denominators

This is the cleanest trap on the page. KVM 1 is badged **67% off**, and that is arithmetically true — but the discount is measured against the **struck-through list price of $19.49**, not against what you will actually pay next:

- Promo vs list: `1 − 6.49 / 19.49 = 66.7%` → the **67% off** badge.
- Renewal vs list: `1 − 11.99 / 19.49 = 38.5%` → the renewal is still discounted off list.
- Renewal vs promo: `11.99 / 6.49 = 1.847` → you pay **+84.7%**, which is the only number that describes your bank account.

So the badge is a real discount off a price almost nobody pays, and the +84.7% is the number that is absent from the card. Same card, three denominators, and only one of them is printed.

### Where "cancel anytime" actually stops

Hostinger ToS §16, verbatim:

> Charge Date depends on the type of Services and length of subscription period. In any case, Hostinger charges the Payment Method linked to your Account before (e. g., from 30 (thirty) to 0 (zero) calendar days before) the end of the current subscription period.

> We have the right, but not an obligation, to inform you via email about the upcoming auto-renewal before the Charge Date (e.g., Customers having subscriptions for 1 (one) month period will not be informed).

Two consequences, both derivable from that text and neither stated on the pricing page:

1. **On a 24-month plan you have until roughly day 700 of 730.** The charge window opens 30 days early, so a cancellation on day 705 of a 730-day term is too late for the *next* charge. "Cancel anytime" means anytime before month 23.
2. **On a 1-month plan the stated window starts at the moment of purchase.** "30 days before the end" of a 30-day term is day zero. Hostinger does not say it charges on day zero — it says the window runs from 30 to 0 days — but it does say, explicitly, that **monthly subscribers will not be emailed about it at all**. Read those two together: for monthly plans there is no guaranteed warning and no guaranteed window.

The same section also lets you add backup payment methods that *"can be charged by Hostinger automatically if your default Payment Method does not work"*. Turning off one card is not the same as turning off the renewal.

## The one escape hatch, and its 180-day lock

If the $287.76 does land, Hostinger's Refund Policy (Last revised 2026-10-02 07:17:59) contains a sentence that most people would not think to look for:

> "Date of the transaction," for the purpose of this Refund Policy, means the date of purchase of any product or service, **which includes the date any renewal is processed** by Hostinger…

A renewal is a fresh transaction with its own **30-day** refund clock. So the auto-renewal you did not want is, in principle, refundable for 30 days after it is charged — KVM VPS is listed under "PRODUCTS AVAILABLE FOR REFUND UNDER STANDARD TERMS".

But the VPS-specific condition two lines down closes it again:

> VPS hosting plan: Refundable only if at the moment of initiation of the refund both the following conditions are met: (i) VPS hosting plan refund is initiated within 30 days from the date of the transaction of that specific VPS hosting plan and (ii) **more than 180 days have passed from the moment of initiation of last refund for any other VPS hosting plan**, if any.

So: **30 days to claim, but at most one VPS refund every 180 days.** If you refunded a VPS in the last six months — including a different VPS, on a different plan — the renewal that fired without warning is not refundable. Note also that "Upgrades for KVM VPS" sit in the non-refundable list, and that anything bought with cryptocurrency is excluded from refunds outright.

## DigitalOcean: no notice, no toggle, and one clause that is not cancelable at all

DigitalOcean's ToS §6.3 (Last Updated 22 Aug 2026) is unusually blunt on both directions:

> By entering into this TOS and using the Services, you agree to be billed on a recurring basis and to be automatically charged by us or our Payment Processors using your Payment Methods upon invoicing.

> You may cancel your Services account at any time through your account settings or by contacting DigitalOcean support to avoid future charges, except as set forth below.

Zero notice period, genuinely. But the sentence after "except as set forth below" is the one that matters on a VPS deal:

> Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the TOS or an order form, your purchase of committed usage, reserved capacity, or a similar consumption commitment (e.g., Required Monthly Usage or a Term Spend Minimum) is **non-cancelable and non-reducible**, and the unpaid remainder of such commitment(s) is **immediately due and payable** as of the date of the cancellation…

That is the opposite of a notice period: cancelling does not end the obligation, it **accelerates** it. If your deal involved a spend commitment, "cancel anytime" converts the remaining balance into a single immediate debt.

There is also no auto-renewal switch to look for, because there is no subscription. Per DigitalOcean's billing docs, *"We automatically invoice and charge your team's or organization's primary payment method on the first day of each month for the previous month's usage, or partway through the month when your balance reaches your tier's auto-charge amount."* You are billed for what already ran. The cancellation lever is **destroying the resource**, not flipping a renewal setting — a distinction that matters, because the deactivation doc (last_updated 2026-07-13) makes account deactivation a separate, gated action: you must first resolve team memberships, *"When you delete a team, you must destroy all resources on the team. The payment method associated with the team is be charged for the team's final balance."* Deactivating the account **stops billing**; it does not delete your servers for you.

Two more asymmetries worth knowing before you rely on "cancel anytime":

- **They can end it faster than you can.** ToS §12: *"While we prefer to give advance notice of termination, we reserve the right… to terminate your access to all or any part of the Websites and/or Services at any time, with or without notice, effective immediately."*
- **Your notice to them has to be posted.** ToS §14.5: notices must be sent *"by certified U.S. Mail or by Federal Express (signature required and return receipt requested)"* to their Broomfield, Colorado address. Support tickets are not the contractual notice channel.
- **Prices are not locked.** ToS §6.1 lets them change prices at any time, and *"By continuing to access or use the Websites or Services on or after the date of the price change, you are agreeing to accept and pay the updated prices"* — with deactivation as your *"sole and exclusive remedy"*.

## Hetzner: the only actual notice period of the three

Hetzner's general Terms and Conditions (Version 2.0.0, last updated 27 October 2021) are the only source here that answers the question in the form it was asked:

> 2.5. Contracts are concluded for an unlimited time period unless otherwise agreed.

> 2.6. The contract may be terminated by either party with **30 days' notice to the end of the month**, without specifying any reasons. Differing periods of notice may apply to the Customers depending on the description of relevant services. Notice of termination may be given in text form by letter, fax, email or via the Customer's account on our secure customer interface.

Three things to pull out of that. First, **30 days to the end of a calendar month is not the same as 30 days** — a notice sent on the 3rd of a month does not start the clock until the month ends, so worst case you are paying for close to two further months. Second, **email counts** as valid notice, which is more forgiving than DigitalOcean's certified-mail requirement. Third, the escape hatch in the middle — *"Differing periods of notice may apply… depending on the description of relevant services"* — means the 30 days is a default, not a guarantee for your specific product.

For US-based customers the appended Special Terms are explicit about the renewal mechanism that the general T&C only implies: *"7. Contract Duration and Termination. The contracts will continue and automatically renew themselves until terminated by either party."* Hetzner can also terminate you *"without notice for good cause"* (§2.7), and reserves the right to change prices with prior notification via the customer account or email (§1.3). Separately, §12.1 grants the EU statutory **14-day** withdrawal right, which is a cooling-off period, not a cancellation route for month 13.

## What the three comparison sites put in front of you instead

Read on 2026-10-12, none of the three answers this question on the page you actually land on:

- **LowEndBox** — the homepage is a filter hub plus card feeds. Cards carry title, author, date, comment count, a blurb and a read-more link. There is **no renewal field, no auto-renewal note, and no cancellation field on any card**. The closest thing to a renewal disclosure anywhere on the first screen is the phrase "First Year" inside a headline.
- **Namecheap** — this one is the most instructive, because the machinery exists and is simply not pointed at VPS. On the same homepage, five promo cards print a renewal line: "Renews from $1.24/mo" (Private Email), "Renews for $9.88/mo" (EasyWP), "Renews at $7.88/mo" (FastVPN), "Renews from $3.88/mo" (Personal Site Maker), "Renews from $8.88/mo" (Business Site Maker). The **VPS card prints "From $3.88 Annual plan / Instead of $4.88/mo" and no renewal line at all**. So Namecheap clearly knows how to disclose a renewal price and declines to do it on the VPS card.
- **Liquid Web** — the VPS packages page is the only one of the three that prints a renewal number, and it is more specific than Hostinger's: *"Introductory price. Renews at $2,004 /year after the initial 1-year term."* (8 GB, $150.30/mo), *"$2,676 /year"* (16 GB, $175.50/mo), *"$5,280 /year"* (32 GB, $256.50/mo). Those divide out to $167, $223 and $440 per month — **+11.1%, +27.1% and +71.5%** over the intro monthly rate, and the three discount badges (10%, 21%, 42% off) are computed against exactly those renewal figures. But the page never uses the words "auto-renew" and states **no cancellation notice period anywhere**.

## Not verifiable (and not guessed)

Consistent with how this series handles unreachable sources: where a page could not be read directly, nothing was filled in from memory, from a cache, or from a proxy.

- **Liquid Web** — `liquidweb.com` returns **403** to a direct request from this machine. The figures above come from reading the public page and are labelled as such; the cancellation and auto-renewal terms on their legal pages were not verified.
- **Namecheap** — `namecheap.com` returns **403** to a direct request. The homepage card figures above are from reading the public page; their VPS auto-renewal setting was not verified.
- **Hetzner Cloud specifically** — `hetzner.com/legal/cloud-terms-and-conditions/` returns only a region-redirect shell with no clause text, so no Cloud-specific deviation from the 30-day default could be confirmed. Given §2.6's own *"Differing periods of notice may apply"*, treat 30 days as the general default rather than a Cloud-specific guarantee.

## What to do with this

1. **Never read "Cancel anytime" as a date.** Convert it: `deadline = term end − 30 days` for Hostinger, `end of a calendar month + 30 days` for Hetzner, `now` for DigitalOcean.
2. **Multiply the renewal rate by the term, not by one month.** A Hostinger KVM 1 renewal is a **$287.76** transaction, not a $11.99 one, because the renewal period matches the period you bought.
3. **Put the deadline in a calendar the day you buy**, not the day before expiry — for a 24-month Hostinger term that is month 23.
4. **If you are on Hostinger monthly, assume no email will arrive.** The ToS says so directly. Check the toggle; do not wait for a warning.
5. **Screenshot the renewal line at checkout.** Hostinger's own ToS reserves the right to change *"Services' renewal fees displayed at this Site at the time of your first purchase"*, effective when the service comes up for renewal. The number on the card is not a promise.
6. **Before signing any DigitalOcean deal with a spend commitment, read it as debt.** Committed usage is *"non-cancelable and non-reducible"* and the unpaid remainder becomes *"immediately due and payable"* on cancellation. That is not a subscription; it is a liability.
7. **Know which lever you are pulling.** On DigitalOcean, destroying the Droplet stops the accrual and deactivating the account stops the billing — they are different actions and only the second one ends charges. On Hostinger and Hetzner, the lever is the toggle or a notice in text form, and only Hetzner requires you to give it 30 days in advance.

articles.title: What a Gigabyte of VPS Disk Actually Costs (NVMe vs SSD, Priced Per GB)
articles.description: Every VPS deal page calls its storage "NVMe" or "SSD" but none of them price it. Read on 2026-10-11, DigitalOcean's own pricing page puts a gigabyte of included disk anywhere from $0.24 to $2.52 a month — a 10.5x spread, and the NVMe badge does not predict where a plan lands. Hostinger sells NVMe at $0.065/GB, which is cheaper than DigitalOcean's non-NVMe SSD.
articles.question: On a VPS deal, how much more does NVMe storage actually cost than SSD, measured per gigabyte?
articles.body:
**The short answer: NVMe costs DigitalOcean about 46% more per gigabyte than its own regular SSD — and that is the only honest number in this article, because at one vendor the spread inside the NVMe-labelled plans alone is 5.77x.** Read on 2026-10-11, `digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets` publishes 31 plans across five families. Divide the monthly price by the included disk and a gigabyte costs anywhere from **$0.24** to **$2.52** per month. That is a **10.5x spread on one vendor's own page**, and the word "NVMe" tells you nothing about where in that range a plan sits.

Meanwhile the cross-vendor number runs the other way entirely. Hostinger sells **400 GB of NVMe for $25.99/mo — $0.065 per GB**. DigitalOcean's plain, non-NVMe SSD is **$0.30 per GiB**. Hostinger's NVMe is **4.6x cheaper per gigabyte than DigitalOcean's regular SSD**, and it is still cheaper if you price Hostinger at its *renewal* rate, which is the worst case.

So the two questions people actually ask — "is NVMe worth it?" and "how much more does NVMe cost?" — have completely different answers, and neither is the one the deal pages imply.

## The formula, so you can check this yourself

Every number below is one division. No estimation, no extrapolation, no scraping a field that does not exist:

```
$ per GB of disk = monthly plan price (USD) ÷ included disk (GB or GiB)
```

One worked example: DigitalOcean's Basic 16 GiB / 8 vCPU plan is listed at **$96.00/mo** with **320 GiB** of SSD. `96.00 ÷ 320 = 0.300`. That plan sells disk at **$0.30/GiB/month**.

Two caveats, stated up front so you can discount the numbers honestly:

1. **This is a bundling metric, not a marginal price.** You are not buying disk alone; you are buying RAM, vCPU, transfer and disk in one package. `$/GB` measures how generously a plan is provisioned with disk relative to its price. It is the right number for comparing two plans, and the wrong number for computing what one extra gigabyte would cost you.
2. **DigitalOcean quotes GiB, Hostinger quotes GB.** 1 GB = 0.931 GiB, so Hostinger's true per-GiB figure is about **7.4% worse** than its per-GB figure. I give both below, because at a 4.6x gap the unit difference does not change any conclusion, but it would be sloppy not to show it.

| Storage-Optimized | 64 GiB | 8 | 1,170 GiB | $524.00 | **$0.4479** |
| Storage-Optimized | 128 GiB | 16 | 2,340 GiB | $1,048.00 | **$0.4479** |
| Storage-Optimized | 192 GiB | 24 | 3,520 GiB | $1,572.00 | **$0.4466** |
| Storage-Optimized | 256 GiB | 32 | 4,690 GiB | $2,096.00 | **$0.4469** |

Three things fall out of that table that no deal page says.

**The NVMe badge does not price the disk.** DigitalOcean's own copy attaches NVMe to four of the five families — Memory-Optimized (*"Memory-Optimized Droplets use NVMe SSDs"*) and Storage-Optimized (*"Storage-Optimized Droplets use NVMe... can be order of magnitude faster than our regular SSDs"*) unconditionally, and CPU-Optimized and General Purpose only on their *"Premium variant"* (*"The Premium variant... also provides up to 10Gbps outbound network speeds and NVMe SSDs"*). Those four NVMe-tagged families charge **$0.4367, $1.6800, $1.6800 and $2.5200** per GiB. The cheapest NVMe and the most expensive NVMe on the page differ by **5.77x**. If you are choosing on the strength of the word "NVMe," you are choosing on a label that spans a 5.77x price range.

**The one clean NVMe-vs-SSD comparison is +45.6%.** Storage-Optimized is the family DigitalOcean commits to NVMe without conditions, and it is the only one that is also genuinely disk-heavy, so it is the only fair comparison against the regular-SSD Basic line. Storage-Optimized runs **$0.4367/GiB**; the Basic line settles at **$0.3000/GiB** from 60 GiB upward. That is a **45.6% premium**. Against Basic's cheapest rung ($0.2400/GiB) the premium is **81.9%**. So: *roughly 46–82%*, depending on which SSD rung you measure from. That is the answer to "how much more does NVMe cost" — and it is a lot less than the marketing implies, because the disk is not what you are paying for.

**The Basic line has no volume discount at all.** From 60 GiB to 320 GiB — a 5.3x increase in disk — the per-GiB price is flat at exactly **$0.3000**. And the smallest plan is the worst deal on the page: the 512 MiB / 10 GiB plan charges **$0.4000/GiB**, 67% more per gigabyte than the 1 GiB plan directly above it. If disk is what you need, the entry plan is the one plan never to buy it in.

## Hostinger: the premium is negative across vendors

Read from `hostinger.com/vps-hosting` on 2026-10-11. Every Hostinger KVM plan states its media explicitly as **"NVMe disk space"** in the plan feature list, and the page's own FAQ gives the prices: *"KVM 1 – $6.49/month, KVM 2 – $8.99/month, KVM 4 – $12.99/month, KVM 8 – $25.99/month."* The renewal rates are printed on the same cards as *"Renews at $11.99/mo for 2 years"* and so on.

| Plan | vCPU | RAM | NVMe disk | Promo $/mo | **$/GB promo** | Renews at | **$/GB renewal** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KVM 1 | 1 | 4 GB | 50 GB | $6.49 | **$0.1298** | $11.99 | **$0.2398** |
| KVM 2 | 2 | 8 GB | 100 GB | $8.99 | **$0.0899** | $14.99 | **$0.1499** |
| KVM 4 | 4 | 16 GB | 200 GB | $12.99 | **$0.0650** | $28.99 | **$0.1449** |
| KVM 8 | 8 | 32 GB | 400 GB | $25.99 | **$0.0650** | $49.99 | **$0.1250** |

Adjusted to GiB, the best tier is **$0.0697/GiB** on promo and **$0.1342/GiB** on renewal.

Now line that up against DigitalOcean:

- **Hostinger's NVMe on promo ($0.0650/GB) is 4.6x cheaper per gigabyte than DigitalOcean's regular SSD ($0.3000/GiB)** — the supposedly premium media, at the lower price.
- **Hostinger's NVMe on promo is 6.7x cheaper than DigitalOcean's NVMe** on Storage-Optimized ($0.4367/GiB).
- **Even at Hostinger's worst renewal rate — $0.2398/GB, the KVM 1 renewal, the least favourable number in that whole table — it still undercuts DigitalOcean's cheapest SSD rung of $0.2400/GiB.** The premium is not small. It is negative.

Two more structural differences worth knowing. Hostinger's per-GB price **falls** as you go up — $0.1298 → $0.0899 → $0.0650, a 2.0x volume discount — while DigitalOcean's Basic line is flat and its premium lines are perfectly flat. And Hostinger provisions **12.50 GB of disk per GB of RAM** on every single plan, against 20–30 on Basic, 6.25 on CPU-Optimized, 3.125 on General Purpose and Memory-Optimized, and 18.3–18.75 on Storage-Optimized. If you want to know how much disk you get for the RAM you are buying, that ratio is the faster test, and it is not printed anywhere.

## The benchmark that makes all of this concrete

The same DigitalOcean page carries an "Additional product pricing" table, and it is the only place on the page where a gigabyte is sold on its own:

- **Droplet Snapshots — $0.06/GB per month.**
- Backups, usage-based — *"start at $0.01/GiB per month."*

Put that next to the bundled figures and the bundling markup becomes visible:

| What you are buying | $/GiB | Multiple of DO's own snapshot rate ($0.06) |
|---|---|---|
| DigitalOcean snapshot storage | $0.06 | 1.0x |
| Hostinger NVMe, promo (KVM 4/8) | $0.0650 | 1.1x |
| DigitalOcean Basic SSD, cheapest | $0.2400 | **4.0x** |
| DigitalOcean Basic SSD, standard | $0.3000 | **5.0x** |
| DigitalOcean Basic SSD, 512 MiB plan | $0.4000 | **6.7x** |
| DigitalOcean Storage-Optimized NVMe | $0.4367 | **7.3x** |
| DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized / Memory-Optimized NVMe | $1.6800 | **28.0x** |
| DigitalOcean General Purpose NVMe | $2.5200 | **42.0x** |

**The most expensive gigabyte DigitalOcean sells is 42x the cheapest gigabyte DigitalOcean sells.** Both are on the same page. One is inside a General Purpose Droplet; the other is a snapshot. If your workload is read-heavy, archival, or anything that does not need block I/O at sub-millisecond latency, the plan upgrade is the expensive way to buy capacity.

There is a second, sharper use for that $0.01/GiB figure. DigitalOcean also offers percentage-based backups at **20% of Droplet cost (weekly)** or **30% (daily)**. Those two pricing models break even when:

```
disk GiB ÷ monthly price = 20   (weekly)   or   30   (daily)
```

No plan on the page gets close. The highest disk-to-price ratio DigitalOcean sells anywhere is **4.167 GiB per $1/month** (the Basic 1 GiB and 2 GiB / 1 vCPU plans); the General Purpose line manages **0.397**. So percentage-based backups are the expensive option on **every single plan published**, by 4.8x at best (Basic 1 GiB) and **50.4x** at worst (General Purpose, where weekly percentage backup of the $63/mo plan costs $12.60/mo against $0.25/mo usage-based). Pick usage-based.

## What I could not verify

Being straight about the holes, because a comparison table that quietly drops the unreadable vendors is worse than no table:

- **Namecheap** — `namecheap.com/hosting/vps/` returned **403** to this site's declared crawler on 2026-10-11. Its homepage advertises VPS *"From $3.88 Annual plan, Instead of $4.88/mo"* with no disk size and no media type at all. **Not verifiable.**
- **Liquid Web** — `liquidweb.com/vps-hosting/packages/` returned **403**. **Not verifiable.**
- **Vultr, Linode (Akamai), Contabo** — all **403**. **Not verifiable.**
- **Hetzner** — `hetzner.com/cloud` returns 200 but renders prices client-side, so no figures are extractable. **Not verifiable.**
- **DigitalOcean's disk-variant selector** (1x / 2x / 3x on the four premium families) is client-side; only the default 1x values are in the served HTML. I did not read the 2x and 3x prices, so this article makes no claim about the marginal price of adding disk within a premium plan.

No proxy, cache, or archive was used to fill any of those gaps, and no figure in this article came from anywhere but the two pages that returned 200.

## What to do with this

1. **Stop treating "NVMe" as a price signal.** Across the plans on one vendor's page it spans 5.77x. Across vendors it is inverted. The word tells you about the controller, not the invoice.
2. **If you can measure the real premium, it is about 46%.** Storage-Optimized NVMe at $0.4367/GiB versus Basic SSD at $0.3000/GiB. Pay that if you need the IOPS; do not pay it because a badge is green.
3. **Run the division before you upgrade.** `monthly price ÷ disk GB`. If you are comparing two plans and one is above $0.30/GB, you are buying RAM and vCPU and calling it storage.
4. **If you only need capacity, do not buy a bigger plan.** At $0.06/GB, snapshot storage is 4x to 42x cheaper than the same vendor's bundled disk, depending on the family.
5. **Buy disk where it is actually cheap.** Hostinger's NVMe at $0.065/GB undercuts DigitalOcean's regular SSD by 4.6x and its NVMe by 6.7x — and still wins at renewal. Check the renewal column before you sign; a promo per-GB number that triples on renewal is not a per-GB number you can plan with.

---

*Figures read 2026-10-11 from `digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets` and `hostinger.com/vps-hosting`, both returning HTTP 200. All per-gigabyte values are the monthly price divided by the included disk as printed on those pages. Vendors returning 403 or client-rendered pages are marked not verifiable and were not filled in from any other source.*

articles.title: What a VPS Deal Actually Costs Per GB of RAM
articles.description: We divided the posted price by the RAM on every plan card three major hosts publish. The spread runs from $1.62 to $9.00 per GB — and one plan inside a single provider's own line costs 50% more per GB than the bigger plan directly above it.
articles.question: How much am I really paying per GB of RAM on a VPS deal, and which plans are quietly the worst value in their own lineup?
articles.body:
Every VPS deal page prints a monthly price. None of them print the price of what you are actually buying. Divide the posted price by the RAM on the card and the same three hosts — read from their own pricing pages on 2026-10-09 — span **$1.62 to $9.00 per GB**, a 5.5x spread on a commodity. Worse: **DigitalOcean sells a 2 GB / 2 vCPU Droplet at $9.00 per GB, while the 4 GB / 2 vCPU directly above it costs $6.00 per GB.** Same CPU count, double the memory, better rate. The smaller plan is strictly worse value than the one above it.

## The table: price divided by RAM

| Provider | Plan | Posted /mo | RAM | vCPU | **$/GB RAM** | $/vCPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hostinger | KVM 1 | $6.49 | 4 GB | 1 | **$1.62** | $6.49 |
| Hostinger | KVM 2 | $8.99 | 8 GB | 2 | **$1.12** | $4.50 |
| Hostinger | KVM 4 | $12.99 | 16 GB | 4 | **$0.81** | $3.25 |
| Hostinger | KVM 8 | $25.99 | 32 GB | 8 | **$0.81** | $3.25 |
| Namecheap | Spark | $3.88 | 1 GB | 1 | **$3.88** | $3.88 |
| Namecheap | Pulsar | $6.88 | 2 GB | 2 | **$3.44** | $3.44 |
| Namecheap | Quasar | $12.88 | 6 GB | 4 | **$2.15** | $3.22 |
| Namecheap | Magnetar | $24.88 | 12 GB | 8 | **$2.07** | $3.11 |
| Namecheap | Hypernova | $46.88 | 24 GB | 12 | **$1.95** | $3.91 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 512 MiB | $4.00 | 0.5 GB | 1 | **$8.00** | $4.00 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 1 GiB | $6.00 | 1 GB | 1 | **$6.00** | $6.00 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 2 GiB | $12.00 | 2 GB | 1 | **$6.00** | $12.00 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 2 GiB / 2 vCPU | $18.00 | 2 GB | 2 | **$9.00** | $9.00 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 4 GiB | $24.00 | 4 GB | 2 | **$6.00** | $12.00 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 8 GiB | $48.00 | 8 GB | 4 | **$6.00** | $12.00 |
| DigitalOcean | Basic 16 GiB | $96.00 | 16 GB | 8 | **$6.00** | $12.00 |

Read the billing basis before you compare: Hostinger's posted rate is the **total for the initial term divided by the months in it**, and its cards print the renewal rate separately. Namecheap's posted rate is the **yearly-billed monthly equivalent**. DigitalOcean posts a straight monthly list rate. These are not the same kind of number, and that is the point — the deal pages put them side by side as if they were.

## The renewal rate is where the unit price breaks

Hostinger prints both numbers, so you can watch the per-GB rate move:

| Plan | Promotional $/GB | Renewal $/GB | Jump |
|---|---|---|---|
| KVM 1 | $1.62 | $3.00 | **1.85x** |
| KVM 2 | $1.12 | $1.87 | **1.67x** |
| KVM 4 | $0.81 | $1.81 | **2.23x** |
| KVM 8 | $0.81 | $1.56 | **1.92x** |

At renewal, Hostinger's entry plan costs **$3.00 per GB** — which lands right next to Namecheap's yearly-billed rate of $3.88 and is no longer the cheapest thing on this page by a wide margin. The discount does not shrink the unit price by a fixed amount. It moves you to a different tier entirely.

Two more things fall out of that column. **KVM 4 and KVM 8 have identical promotional unit prices** — $0.81 per GB and $3.25 per vCPU each. Buying the bigger plan gets you no per-unit discount at all during the promotional term; the difference only appears at renewal ($1.81 vs $1.56). And the worst renewal jump is on KVM 4, not on the entry plan.

## DigitalOcean's line is flat — except in one place

Across 1 GB, 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB and 16 GB, DigitalOcean's Basic Droplets hold an almost perfectly flat **$6.00 per GB**. Whatever you think of the absolute number, that is a legible pricing curve: double the memory, double the price, no games.

Then there are the two exceptions, and one of them is a trap:

- The **512 MiB** plan costs $8.00 per GB — the second-worst rate in this entire table.
- The **2 GiB / 2 vCPU** plan costs **$9.00 per GB**, which is worse than every other DigitalOcean plan on the page *and* worse than the 4 GiB / 2 vCPU plan sitting directly below it at $6.00 per GB.

Both have 2 vCPUs. One has twice the memory. The one with twice the memory is 33% cheaper per GB. There is no workload for which the $18 plan is the better buy.

## Why nobody publishes this number

We read 30 pages across the three biggest comparison sites ranking for VPS deals. Not one of them divides price by RAM. They rank by headline monthly price, by star rating, or by a feature checklist — all of which are things the provider controls and prints for you.

Price per GB is the one number the provider does not print, cannot spin, and does not want compared. Hostinger will tell you it is "67% off." It will not tell you that at renewal you are paying $3.00 per GB, or that KVM 8 gives you no per-unit advantage over KVM 4 for the entire promotional term.

## How to run this on any deal in ten seconds

```
$/GB RAM  = monthly price / RAM in GB
$/vCPU    = monthly price / vCPU count
```

Then do the thing the deal pages will not do for you: **compute it twice**, once at the promotional rate and once at the renewal rate printed on the same card. If the renewal column is not printed, treat the promotional unit price as temporary and reprice at the list rate before you commit.

And check the plan one size up. In every lineup above, per-GB price falls as you scale — except where it does not, and those are exactly the plans to skip.

## What we could not verify

Hetzner's Cloud pricing page renders its plan prices client-side and returned no figures to an automated reader on 2026-10-09, so it is absent from the table rather than estimated. Its published billing model is hourly with a monthly price cap, rounded up to whole hours — a different shape from the three above, and worth its own calculation once the plan figures are readable.

Vultr, Linode and Contabo pricing pages also refused automated reads today. We are not filling those rows with recalled numbers.

articles.title: Cheap VPS Deals: How Long Your Data Survives After You Cancel — and the One Copy Each Host Keeps
articles.description: Read off five hosts' own pages on 2026-10-18: not one of them publishes a retention period for your VPS disk. What they publish is a retention period for backups only — DigitalOcean 4 weeks for weekly and 7 days for daily, Hetzner 7 rolling slots, Namecheap one weekly copy that overwrites itself — and a moment of deletion. Hetzner writes it out plainly: 'we will immediately delete your data... We cannot recover your data after you cancel the product.' Namecheap will erase 'at once' on request. Hostinger may 'destroy any data and files (including back-up copies)' with 'no obligation to provide.' Plus the arithmetic that actually saves you: on every one of DigitalOcean's 29 Standard/Intel/AMD tiers, a permanent snapshot of a full disk costs less than switching on 7-day daily backups — 1.06x to 1.96x less.
articles.question: If I cancel or destroy a cheap VPS, how long does the host keep my data, and can I get it back afterwards?
articles.body:
**Read off five hosts' own pages on 2026-10-18: zero of them publish a retention period for your VPS disk. Not one.** What they publish is (a) a retention period for *backups* — and only backups — and (b) a *moment* of deletion. Hetzner is the only one that writes the moment down in plain words: *"After you have finished the cancellation, we at Hetzner will immediately delete your data... We cannot recover your data after you cancel the product."* Namecheap offers you a button that erases *"at once."* Hostinger reserves the right to *"remove and destroy any data and files (including back-up copies)"* with *"no obligation to provide you with such data and files."* DigitalOcean's answer is a sentence most people only read after it is too late: *"If you have neither snapshots nor backups, then we do not have a backup of your Droplet's data available in our system."*

So the real question is not "how long do they keep it." It is **"which one copy is mine, and does it outlive the machine?"** On every host in this comparison the answer is the same shape: automatic backups are *bound to the server and die with it*, while a manually-created snapshot is *yours until you delete it and survives the server's death*. That single distinction — not the price, not the RAM — is what decides whether cancelling a $4/month VPS costs you nothing or costs you everything.

## The survival table — the whole article in one grid

| Host | Automatic backups | Do they survive deleting the server? | Manual snapshot | Published retention for the disk itself |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DigitalOcean** | Weekly or daily (also 4/6/12-hourly on usage-based plans) | **No** — must be converted to a snapshot first | Yes, kept until you delete it | **None published** |
| **Hetzner** | Daily, **7 slots** | **No** — *"automatically be deleted if you delete the server"* | Yes — *"remain available even if you delete the server"* | **None** — deletion is *"immediately"* |
| **Namecheap** | Weekly, **during the weekend**, overwritten by the next one | Effectively **no** — one rolling copy | Not offered on VPS | **None** — *"canceled at once and all the data erased immediately"* |
| **Hostinger** | Not documented publicly for VPS | Not documented | Not documented | **None** — *"destroy any data and files (including back-up copies)"* |
| **Liquid Web** | Acronis, **daily**, 100/250/500 GB by tier | Not published | Not mentioned on the page | **None published** |

Two things to notice. First, the "snapshot survives, backup dies" split is identical at DigitalOcean and Hetzner — the two hosts that actually document it. Second, the only host that tells you *when* the disk goes is Hetzner, and its answer is "immediately."

## How far back can you actually roll?

This is the number people think they are buying when they tick "enable backups." It is almost always smaller than they think, because **retention windows and restore points are two different things.**

| Host / plan | How often | How long kept | How many restore points | Worst-case data loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DigitalOcean weekly | Weekly | **4 weeks** | **4** | 7 days |
| DigitalOcean daily | Daily | **7 days** | **7** | 24 hours |
| DigitalOcean usage-based | You choose (4h/6h/12h/daily/weekly) | **Custom** — you set it | Varies | Down to 4 hours |
| Hetzner Backups | Daily | 7 slots | **7** | 24 hours |
| Hetzner Snapshots | Manual | Until you delete it | Up to **30** across all projects | Whatever you last took |
| Namecheap VPS | Weekly, at the weekend | Overwritten each week | **1** | 7 days |
| Namecheap VPS + Complete Management | 3× per week, 100 GB included | Overwritten | 3 per week | ~2–3 days |
| Liquid Web (Acronis) | Daily | **Not published** | Not published | Unknown |

The trap is DigitalOcean weekly: *4 weeks* sounds like the safest option in the table, and it is the longest window — but it only ever holds **4** copies, so your worst case is a full week of missing writes. Daily gives you the same worst case (24 hours) with a *shorter* window. **Length of window and frequency of protection are independent, and the marketing names only tell you one of them.**

Hetzner's 7 slots and DigitalOcean's 7 days are the same number by two different routes: Hetzner caps by *count*, DigitalOcean caps by *age*. If you ever create extra backups on Hetzner, the count cap bites first — *"If all slots are full and you create an additional one, then the oldest Backup will be deleted."*

## The money math: the permanent copy is cheaper than the 7-day copy

This is the part nobody publishes, because it makes the upsell look silly. DigitalOcean prices backups as a **percentage of the Droplet** and snapshots as a **flat rate per GB**. Those two curves cross, and they cross in a place that is almost always on the snapshot's side.

- Backups, Basic plans: **20.0%** of the Droplet's cost per month (weekly), **30.0%** (daily).
- Snapshots: **$0.06 per GB per month**, minimum charge $0.01.

Break-even, solved for the disk you actually use:

```
0.30 × monthly_price  =  0.06 × used_GB
        used_GB       =  5 × monthly_price
```

**If the GB you are using is less than 5× your monthly Droplet price, a snapshot that lasts forever costs less than daily backups that expire in 7 days.**

Run it across every Standard / Intel / AMD tier on DigitalOcean's pricing page as read on 2026-10-18 (snapshot costed at a *full* disk — the most unfavourable case, since DO bills snapshots on actual disk usage):

| Droplet | Disk | $/mo | Daily backups (30%) | Full-disk snapshot @ $0.06/GB | Snapshot is cheaper by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 MiB / 1 vCPU | 10 GiB (10.74 GB) | $4.00 | $1.20 | $0.64 | **1.86x** |
| 1 GiB / 1 vCPU | 25 GiB (26.84 GB) | $6.00 | $1.80 | $1.61 | **1.12x** |
| 2 GiB / 1 vCPU | 50 GiB (53.69 GB) | $12.00 | $3.60 | $3.22 | **1.12x** |
| 2 GiB / 2 vCPU | 60 GiB (64.42 GB) | $18.00 | $5.40 | $3.87 | **1.40x** |
| 4 GiB / 2 vCPU | 80 GiB (85.90 GB) | $24.00 | $7.20 | $5.15 | **1.40x** |
| 8 GiB / 4 vCPU | 160 GiB (171.80 GB) | $48.00 | $14.40 | $10.31 | **1.40x** |
| 16 GiB / 8 vCPU | 320 GiB (343.60 GB) | $96.00 | $28.80 | $20.62 | **1.40x** |

Across **all 29 Standard, Intel and AMD tiers** listed on the page, the ratio runs from **1.06x to 1.96x** — the snapshot wins on every single one. The margin is thinnest on the 1 GiB and 2 GiB tiers (1.12x) and widest on the AMD 8 GiB / 2 vCPU tier (1.96x).

Two caveats, stated honestly. Snapshots are a *manual* action — a snapshot you forget to take protects nothing, whereas backups run on a clock. And the table charges the snapshot for a completely full disk; at realistic usage it is cheaper still, because DO says snapshots of Droplets are *"a best estimate based on the disk usage."*

The flip side matters too: usage-based backup plans price *per GiB* rather than as a percentage, and they get **cheaper the more often you back up** — $0.04/GiB weekly down to **$0.01/GiB** every 4 hours. That is a **4.0x spread** in the opposite direction from what intuition suggests, because you are paying for restorable file size, not for frequency.

## DigitalOcean's own two pages disagree — assume the shorter one

This is worth knowing before you rely on any of it. DigitalOcean's *How to Destroy a Droplet* page says:

> "Destroying a Droplet does not destroy its automated backups. Automated backups remain for **four weeks** after creation and then expire."

Its *How do I recover a deleted Droplet?* page says the backups *"remain available until the end of their retention period, which is **four weeks** for weekly backups, **seven days** for daily backups."*

Both are official and both are live. Read together, the safe assumption is **7 days if you were on daily**, because that is the number the recovery page — the one you would actually be using — commits to. The 4-week figure on the destroy page is the weekly-plan number stated without its qualifier. **Plan for 7, not 28.** The gap is 4x.

The escape hatch is explicit and it is free to know:

> "You can convert backups into snapshots to save the image indefinitely."

## Hetzner: the deletion clock depends on which day you click cancel

Hetzner's 30-days-to-the-end-of-the-month policy (doc ID GE-DB2BC) is the only cancellation rule in this comparison that produces a *date*. The rule: add 30 days to your cancellation date, then roll forward to the end of that month. Because the roll-forward crosses a month boundary, the result is **not a fixed 30 days** — and it is not even monotonic.

```
Let D  = day you cancel
    L  = days in the month you cancel
    L2 = days in the following month

If D + 30 <= L :  days = L - D
Else           :  days = (L - D) + L2
```

Worked from Hetzner's own three examples:

| Cancelling on | +30 days lands on | Takes effect | Total runway |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 May | 31 May (still May) | 31 May | **30 days** |
| 17 May | 16 June | 30 June | **44 days** |
| 29 May | 28 June | 30 June | **32 days** |

Now extend the same rule to its extremes:

- **1 May → 30 days.** (1 + 30 = 31, still within May's 31 days.)
- **2 May → 59 days.** (2 + 30 = 1 June, which rolls to 30 June.)
- **1 April → 60 days.** (1 + 30 = 1 May, which rolls to 31 May.)

So the spread is **30 to 60 days — a 2.0x difference — decided entirely by which day of the month you click.** Cancelling on 1 May gives you 30 days; cancelling on 2 May gives you 59. **A one-day difference in when you click is a 29-day difference in when your data dies.**

And when it does take effect, Hetzner's cancellation overview (doc ID GE-4A989, last changed 2026-08-06) is unambiguous:

> "After you have finished the cancellation, we at Hetzner will immediately delete your data. So please be absolutely sure that you want to cancel your product. **We cannot recover your data after you cancel the product.**"

There is no grace period after that sentence. Which means on Hetzner the runway above *is* your export window, and you can add up to 29 days to it for the price of waiting one day before you cancel.

## Namecheap: 7 days, 23 days, or instantly — your choice, and the default is not the safe one

Namecheap's *Hosting packages life cycle* (KB 10567) gives the cleanest timeline in this comparison:

- Invoiced **7 days** before the billing date.
- An "Alert" flag appears **15 days** before expiry on 1- and 3-month cycles, **30 days** before on annual and 2-year cycles.
- If the invoice is still unpaid after the billing date: *"your hosting account will be suspended and cancelled **7 days** later (for Shared packages, VPS and Dedicated server) and **23 days** later (for Reseller packages)"* — a **3.29x** difference by product line.

But the cancellation article (KB 170) describes two completely different paths, and only one of them is what most people mean by "cancel":

1. **Default:** turn off auto-renew and let it expire — the package is suspended, then cancelled.
2. **On request:** *"if you wish to have your hosting package canceled at once and **all the data erased immediately**, you may submit a cancellation request."*

Both are one click in the same Manage screen. **If you cancel the VPS intending to come back for your data later, you have chosen the path that erases it now.**

What recovery looks like if you do lose it (KB 9197, updated 5/9/2025):

- VPS server backups are *"generated once a week, during the weekend"* and *"are over-written by newly created ones"* → **one copy, up to 7 days stale.**
- Restoring gives you *"a new IP address."* If anything hardcoded the old IP, restoration is not the end of the job.
- Data-only retrieval — getting your files *without* rebuilding the VPS — costs **$15** added to your Namecheap balance.
- Extra backup space on Complete Management: **$10 per 10 GB = $1.00/GB**, on top of 100 GB included.
- Dedicated servers: *"all data is deleted from the server,"* and it is *"impossible to obtain a backup for User-Responsible servers or servers with the Basic Management option."*

One genuinely counterintuitive line in that same article: external backup storage is **500 GB for Advanced** servers but **200 GB for Complete Management** servers. The higher management tier ships with **2.5x less** backup space.

## Hostinger publishes four retention numbers — none of them for your VPS disk

Hostinger is the clearest example of the pattern. Its privacy policy has a whole section titled *Retention and Deletion*, and it is full of specific, auditable numbers:

| What | Retention |
|---|---|
| Call and meeting recordings | **30 days** |
| Communication data (emails, requests) | **90 days** |
| Data from accounts suspended for safety | **up to one (1) year** |
| De-personalised profile after account closure (email rewritten to `user@deleted.com`) | as long as legally required (tax, accounting, AML) |

Then there is the disk. Hostinger's Universal Terms of Service gives it no number at all — only a right:

> "Hostinger may, in its sole and absolute discretion, remove and destroy any data and files (**including back-up copies**) stored by you on its servers, and has **no obligation to provide you with such data and files**."

Read those side by side and the shape of the whole market appears: **the retention periods that get published are the ones the host needs for its own compliance. The retention period you need is the one nobody writes down.** Hostinger will tell you exactly how long it keeps a recording of a support call (30 days) and will not tell you how long it keeps your server.

## Liquid Web: you can only back up part of the machine

Liquid Web's VPS page (read 2026-10-18) bundles Acronis backups into every package — *"Daily backups are configured for you and scale automatically with your package"* — and publishes the capacity per tier. Compare that capacity against the disk it is meant to protect:

| Package | vCPU / RAM / Disk | Acronis backup included | Backup ÷ disk | Disk you cannot back up |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 GB | 4 vCPU / 8 GB / **240 GB** | **100 GB** | **41.7%** | **140 GB (58.3%)** |
| 16 GB | 6 vCPU / 16 GB / **440 GB** | **250 GB** | **56.8%** | **190 GB (43.2%)** |
| 32 GB | 8 vCPU / 32 GB / **640 GB** | **500 GB** | **78.1%** | **140 GB (21.9%)** |

**On the entry VPS, the included backup covers 41.7% of the disk.** Fill the machine and you are running unprotected on 58.3% of it. The ratio improves as you climb — 56.8%, then 78.1% — so backup coverage is a *tier feature*, not a baseline.

The page states no retention period, no snapshot capability, and nothing about data after cancellation. **Not verifiable:** Liquid Web's policies pages (`/policies/terms-of-service/` and `/legal/terms-of-service/`) returned a Cloudflare human-verification challenge to our direct requests on 2026-10-18, and per our own rules we did not attempt to work around it — so no claim about Liquid Web's post-cancellation data handling is made in this article beyond what its public VPS page states above.

## What the three comparison sites show you first

Checked on 2026-10-18, on the exact pages people land on:

- **LowEndBox** — homepage cards carry title, author, date, comment count and a teaser; provider, RAM, price and region appear only inside the free-text title, when they appear at all. **Zero** mentions of backups, snapshots, retention, or what happens to data after cancellation.
- **Namecheap** — the homepage has **no VPS card at all**; VPS is a navigation link only. Cards that *are* shown (EasyWP, Private Email, .com, Stellar) print promo and renewal prices. **Zero** mentions of backups, snapshots, retention or cancellation data handling.
- **Liquid Web** — `/vps-hosting/packages/` is the most informative of the three: it does name backups ("Automated backups", Acronis with per-tier GB). But it publishes **no retention period, no snapshot feature, and no cancellation or termination data policy.**

So the answer to "how long do they keep my data" is not available on any of the three first screens, and on only one of the five hosts' own documentation.

## Budget the clock before you cancel

One last practical number. DigitalOcean states that creating a snapshot or backup takes *"about 1 to 3 minutes per GB of used disk space"*, and gives the worked case: *"a Droplet with 10 GB of used disk space would take 10 to 30 minutes."*

That is a real, schedulable cost. On a 10 GB disk you need to decide to leave **20 minutes before** you destroy anything — and on a 320 GiB disk at the 3-minute end you are looking at several hours. Nobody loses data because they forgot to click; they lose it because they clicked destroy first and took the snapshot never.

## What to actually do

1. **Take a manual snapshot before you touch anything.** It is the only artefact at DigitalOcean and Hetzner that outlives the server. Hetzner says snapshots *"remain available even if you delete the server a Snapshot was taken of"*; DigitalOcean says you can *"convert backups into snapshots to save the image indefinitely."* Automatic backups do not count: on Hetzner they are *"automatically deleted if you delete the server."*
2. **On DigitalOcean, prefer the snapshot to daily backups on price alone** if your used GB is under **5× your monthly price** — true on all 29 tiers today (1.06x–1.96x cheaper). You get a longer retention for less money; the only thing you give up is automation.
3. **On Hetzner, look at a calendar before you cancel.** Cancelling on the 1st of a 31-day month gives you 30 days; cancelling one day later gives you 59. Same click, 29 extra days of runway. Deletion is immediate when the clock runs out, and it is not reversible.
4. **On Namecheap, do not use "Cancel Service" if you want your data.** That path erases *"at once."* Let it expire instead, and remember the VPS backup is one weekly copy made at the weekend — up to 7 days stale — and restoration hands you a **new IP**.
5. **Budget the snapshot time:** 1–3 minutes per GB of used space. Decide before you destroy, not after.
6. **If you are on Liquid Web's entry VPS, assume 58.3% of your disk is unprotected** unless you have reduced usage to fit the 100 GB included.

The general rule that survives every host in this comparison: **automatic backups are a feature of the server; a snapshot is a thing you own.** The first one is priced as a percentage and expires on a clock. The second one is priced per gigabyte and expires when you say so. On cheap VPS deals, where the whole machine costs less than a month of the data sitting on it, that is the only line item worth reading twice.

articles.title: What a VPS Hourly Rate Actually Costs Per Month (The Multiplier Is 672, Not 730)
articles.description: Every VPS hourly-to-monthly conversion you have read multiplies by 730. DigitalOcean's own pricing table divides to exactly 672 on all 19 published plan pairs, and its billing docs say cycles run on the calendar month — which means the shortcut is right for uncapped plans, 8.63% too high for capped ones, and hands you 696 free hours a year.
articles.question: On a VPS deal, what does an hourly rate actually cost per month — is the multiplier 730, 672, or something else?
articles.body:
The multiplier is **not** 730. On DigitalOcean's own pricing page, read on 2026-10-10, every one of the 19 published plan pairs divides to **exactly 672 hours** — not 730, not 744, not "about 700." A $0.00595/hr Droplet is listed at $4.00/mo, and 4.00 ÷ 0.00595 = 672.3. A $1.87500/hr General Purpose Droplet is listed at $1,260.00/mo, and 1260.00 ÷ 1.875 = 672.0. Nineteen pairs, one number.

That matters because 730 is the number everyone uses, and using it on the wrong kind of plan overstates your bill by **8.63%** every single month. The catch — and this is the part no pricing page explains — is that 672 is not the same thing as 730 in disguise. They are two different billing contracts:

- **Capped plans** bill a flat monthly ceiling. DigitalOcean states it directly: *"Bundled Plans have a monthly cap, so you'll never pay more than the flat monthly price for that plan."* For these, your real annual cost is **12 × the monthly price**, period. Multiplying the hourly rate by anything is the wrong operation.
- **Uncapped plans** bill actual hours. Same page, next sentence: *"v5 Droplets are billed on actual hours used each month and are not capped at 672 hours."* For these, ×730 *is* correct, because 730 × 12 = 8,760, which is exactly the number of hours in a 365-day year.

So the folk rule everyone repeats is half right: **×730 is the correct formula for uncapped hourly billing and a 8.63% overestimate for capped plans.** The only way to know which one you are looking at is to read the one sentence the pricing page buries in its FAQ — and then to notice that 672 is not an arbitrary constant at all.

## Why 672: it is February

672 hours is exactly 28 days. DigitalOcean's billing documentation pins the cycle to the calendar: *"DigitalOcean billing cycles are monthly. Your balance accrues over the course of the calendar month based on the cost of the resources you use."*

Calendar months are not all the same length, and 2026 is not a leap year. Run a capped Droplet 24/7 for a full year and here is what the collision produces:

| Month type (2026) | Months | Hours in month | Hours billed (capped) | Free hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 31 days | 7 (Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec) | 744 | 672 | **72** |
| 30 days | 4 (Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov) | 720 | 672 | **48** |
| 28 days | 1 (Feb) | 672 | 672 | **0** |

Add it up: 7 × 72 + 4 × 48 = **696 hours of free compute per year**, which is 29 full days. You run 8,760 hours and pay for 8,064. The advertised hourly rate is, quite literally, the **February rate** — the one month of the year where the cap and the calendar agree. In every other month the effective hourly rate is lower than the number printed on the page: in a 31-day month, $4.00 ÷ 744 = **$0.005376/hr** against an advertised $0.00595/hr, a 9.68% discount you get for free.

An uncapped v5 Droplet gets none of that. In January it is billed 744 hours. In February, 672.

## The whole published table, and what ×730 does to it

Every figure below is printed on DigitalOcean's pricing page as of 2026-10-10. The last two columns are the two answers to "what does this cost per month" — and they only agree in February.

| Plan (Shared) | Advertised $/hr | Listed $/mo | $/hr × 730 | Error vs listed | Real annual, capped | Real annual, uncapped |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 MiB / 1 vCPU | $0.00595 | $4.00 | $4.34 | **+8.6%** | $48.00 | $52.12 |
| 1 GiB / 1 vCPU | $0.00893 | $6.00 | $6.52 | **+8.6%** | $72.00 | $78.23 |
| 2 GiB / 1 vCPU | $0.01786 | $12.00 | $13.04 | **+8.6%** | $144.00 | $156.45 |
| 2 GiB / 2 vCPU | $0.02679 | $18.00 | $19.56 | **+8.7%** | $216.00 | $234.68 |
| 4 GiB / 2 vCPU | $0.03571 | $24.00 | $26.07 | **+8.6%** | $288.00 | $312.82 |
| 8 GiB / 4 vCPU | $0.07143 | $48.00 | $52.14 | **+8.6%** | $576.00 | $625.73 |
| 16 GiB / 8 vCPU | $0.14286 | $96.00 | $104.29 | **+8.6%** | $1,152.00 | $1,251.45 |

The same 672 constant holds across the other two families on the page, so it is not a rounding artifact of the cheap tiers:

| Family | Sample pair | $/hr | $/mo | $/mo ÷ $/hr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU-Optimized | 4 GiB / 2 vCPU | $0.06250 | $42.00 | 672.0 |
| CPU-Optimized | 64 GiB / 32 vCPU | $1.00000 | $672.00 | 672.0 |
| General Purpose | 8 GiB / 2 vCPU | $0.09375 | $63.00 | 672.0 |
| General Purpose | 160 GiB / 40 vCPU | $1.87500 | $1,260.00 | 672.0 |

The error in the ×730 column is constant at 730 ÷ 672 − 1 = **8.63%**, on every tier, at every price point. That is the signature of a systematic mistake, not a rounding difference.

## The decision rule you can actually apply

You cannot tell which contract you have from the price. You have to read one sentence. Here is the test:

| What the page says | Your plan is | Monthly cost formula | Annual cost formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| Has a "monthly cap" / "never pay more than the flat monthly price" | **Capped** | The listed monthly price. Stop. | 12 × monthly price |
| "Billed on actual hours used" / "not capped" | **Uncapped** | $/hr × hours in *this* month (672 / 720 / 744) | $/hr × 8,760 |
| No hourly rate published at all | **Neither — it is a term contract** | Ignore hourly entirely; compare total contract value | See below |

That third row is where most VPS deals actually live, and it is worth saying plainly: **if a host does not publish an hourly rate, there is no hourly math to do.** Hostinger's VPS page, read on 2026-10-10, publishes no hourly figure anywhere — it lists KVM 1 at **$6.49/mo** (from $19.49, "67% off"), "Renews at $11.99/mo for 2 years," KVM 2 at $8.99/mo and KVM 4 at $12.99/mo. Namecheap goes the other direction and leads with a monthly-equivalent of an annual charge: its VPS card shows **$3.88/mo**, "Billed yearly," "You pay $46.56 — renews at $58.56/year," with a struck-through "Was $4.88/mo." Both of those reconcile correctly on their own terms (3.88 × 12 = 46.56; 58.56 ÷ 12 = 4.88). Neither has an hourly rate to convert.

Two hosts we could not verify today, stated as such rather than filled in with remembered numbers: direct requests to `liquidweb.com/vps-hosting/packages/` and `vultr.com/pricing/` both returned **HTTP 403** on 2026-10-10, and Hetzner's Cloud page renders its prices client-side, returning placeholder text in place of figures. **Not verifiable.** We did not substitute figures from any cache, proxy or archive for these three.

## Why nobody tells you this

We read the first screen of the three biggest VPS deal destinations on 2026-10-10, and the pattern is consistent: **all of them show a price with a period label attached and none of them reconcile the periods.**

- **LowEndBox** mixes annual and monthly headline prices in the same feed — *"a 1GB VPS for $12/Year"* next to *"a 6GB VPS for Only €3.49 / Month!"* — and never converts one into the other. Hourly billing appears exactly once, as a headline label on a LowEndTalk offer: *"Hourly Billing."* No rate, no conversion, no explanation.
- **Namecheap** leads with $3.88/mo while billing yearly, and shows both the annual total and the renewal rate without ever writing the sentence that connects them.
- **Liquid Web** is monthly-only on its packages page, with 1-year and 2-year toggles and a renewal figure in the fine print. No hourly rate appears anywhere on the screen.

The gap is not that these sites lack the arithmetic. It is that a page whose job is to rank deals cannot stop to explain the units, because explaining the units makes comparable things look less comparable. A $12/year VPS and a €3.49/month VPS are not the same kind of object, and an hourly rate is not a monthly price divided by 730.

## What to do with this

1. **Stop using ×730 on capped plans.** If the plan has a monthly cap, your monthly cost is the monthly price. On the $96.00/mo tier, ×730 tells you $104.29 — $8.29/month, $99.45/year, of pure arithmetic error.
2. **Find the sentence.** "Monthly cap" or "not capped" — it is usually in the FAQ at the bottom of the pricing page, not in the table. That one sentence is worth 8.63%.
3. **For uncapped plans, use 8,760 hours per year, not 730 × 12 as a guess.** They are the same number, but writing it as 8,760 forces you to remember February is cheaper than January: 672 hours billed vs 744.
4. **If you are comparing a capped plan against an uncapped one, compare annual totals, not hourly rates.** The capped plan's advertised hourly rate is its February rate — the most expensive rate it will ever charge you. The uncapped plan's advertised hourly rate is its every-month rate. Comparing $0.00595 against $0.00595 across those two contract types is comparing a ceiling to an average.
5. **When there is no hourly rate, walk away from the hourly question.** Hostinger, Namecheap and Liquid Web deals are term contracts. The number that matters is the renewal price and the total contract value, and no amount of hour arithmetic will get you there.

articles.title: Cheap VPS Deals: Which Hosts Will Ask for Your ID — and What Each One Wants First
articles.description: Read off the providers' own pages on 2026-10-16: Namecheap publishes a list of 18 document types it may request (6 of them, 33.3%, are photo IDs) and gives you a Veriff link that expires in 7 days. Hetzner offers exactly 2 verification paths, 1 of which needs a government ID — and warns that signing up over a VPN makes it harder for them to verify you. Hostinger reserves the right to demand 'government-issued photo identification' and, after a chargeback, a credit-card photo with the first 6 and last 4 digits uncovered — 10 of 16 digits, 62.5% of the number. DigitalOcean's ToS mentions government ID zero times and instead verifies your payment instrument for $0, $5 or $25.00. Liquid Web checks your credit, not your ID.
articles.question: Do I have to hand over a passport or ID to buy a cheap VPS deal, and what happens if I refuse?
articles.body:
**Read off the providers' own pages on 2026-10-16, there is no such thing as a standard VPS signup check: of the five hosts below, two can ask you for a government photo ID (Namecheap, Hostinger), one offers you a choice between an ID document and a non-refundable prepayment (Hetzner), one never mentions government ID anywhere in its terms (DigitalOcean), and one checks your creditworthiness instead of your identity (Liquid Web).** The consequence is also not standardised: Namecheap gives you **7 days** on a Veriff link, Hetzner can simply reject your order, Hostinger can suspend the account, and DigitalOcean's Terms of Service §6.3 lets it bill you "an amount up to your current balance at any time to verify the accuracy of your account information."

That last point is the one nobody writes about. "Do I need ID?" is the wrong question, because only two of these five hosts actually ask it. The useful question is **what each host checks instead of you** — your document, your credit, or your payment instrument — and which of those three you are willing to hand over.

## The trigger matrix, read off official pages on 2026-10-16

| Host | Can demand a government photo ID? | What triggers it | What you hand over | Deadline published? | If you don't |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Namecheap** | **Yes** — Universal Terms of Service: "government-issued photo identification and/or government-issued business identification, plus whatever else we deem required and necessary" | Domain ownership dispute; account access issue; abuse claims; "or various types of abuse claims" | Photo of the ID (both sides) + a selfie, via **Veriff** | **Yes — 7 days**. "the link is valid for 7 days only" | Not stated on the page |
| **Hetzner** | **Yes, on one of two paths** — "a copy of a valid government-issued ID (e.g., ID card or passport)" | Fraud prevention at registration **or** before an order is processed | ID copy **or** an advance payment with your own credit card | **No deadline published** | Order "may not automatically process" or be rejected; account can be rejected for incomplete/false information |
| **Hostinger** | **Yes, at its discretion** — "government-issued business identification or government-issued photo identification" | "reason to believe that your Account information ... is inaccurate, outdated, incomplete or unjustified"; **or** a chargeback | Supporting documents; after a chargeback, "proof of the payment" or a censored card photo | **No deadline published** | "to suspend or terminate your Account" |
| **DigitalOcean** | **No** — zero occurrences of "government" + ID in the ToS | Adding a payment method | The instrument, not the person: $0 / $5 / $25.00 authorisation | Card preauth holds "up to 7 days"; ACH micro-deposits confirmed "within ten days" | Payment method not verified → not usable |
| **Liquid Web** | **No** — no identity check for account opening | "continuing approval of your creditworthiness" | "financial information as we may reasonably request" | **15 days** to cure a suspension before it becomes termination for cause | "We reserve the right to refuse to provide you with our Services in our sole discretion and without notice" |

Two things jump out of that table. First, **the hosts that can demand an ID are the cheap end of the market** — Namecheap's VPS card starts at $3.88/mo annual and Hostinger's KVM line is a promo-driven product, while the two that never ask (DigitalOcean, Liquid Web) are billing $4.00/mo and $150.30/mo respectively. Second, **only one of the five publishes a clock**. Namecheap's 7 days is the only number on the board.

## Hetzner: two paths, and the "no ID" one costs you money

Hetzner's fraud-prevention FAQ is the most explicit document any of these hosts publishes, and it describes exactly **two** ways to verify:

> "**Verification via ID document:** You provide us with a copy of a valid government-issued ID (e.g., ID card or passport). This allows us to confirm that the information provided during registration matches your identity.
> **Verification via prepayment (credit card):** Alternatively, you can verify your account by making an advance payment with your own credit card."

So **1 of the 2 published paths (50%) requires a government ID**, and the other one is a payment. But read the refund condition on that second path before you pick it:

> "As a general rule, we can only refund unused credit that you added during the account verification process if you completely close the account and no outstanding invoices remain."

And: "We do not issue an invoice for credit top-ups (prepayment). We issue invoices only after we provide the service."

That is the trap in the "I don't want to send my passport" argument. The ID-free route is not free — it is **a deposit you cannot withdraw while you remain a customer.** Verification is also not a one-time event at signup: "As part of our fraud prevention measures, we may ask you to verify your account **before we process an order**." You can register successfully and still be stopped at the till.

Hetzner also publishes the only actionable anti-verification advice any host gives, and it is the opposite of what most buyers do:

> "Please, if it is possible, do not use a free email address ... And during the registration process, do not use a VPN service. VPNs make it more difficult for our team to verify your identity and assess the risk of fraud."

Its registration requirements list **four** items — "a valid email address", "personal or business contact information", "a billing address", and "optionally, a phone number for advanced verification". Only **1 of the 4 (25%)** is optional, and that one is the phone, explicitly labelled as being for verification rather than contact.

One more trigger Hetzner documents that no other host does — **order size**: "For first-time customers, we check whether or not the number and value of the products they order seem plausible ... we may not automatically process these orders or may reject them." Its own workaround is to start small: "we suggest that you try one of our lower-priced servers from our Server Auction ... or one of our smaller cloud servers ... for your first order."

## Namecheap: 18 documents, 6 of which are photo IDs

Namecheap's KB article "Why we can request the documents and what they will be" is the longest public KYC list in this group. It enumerates **18** document types:
