Passport · Identity card · Permanent resident card · Health Insurance card with photo (Canada, USA, Australia) · Driver's license · U.S. Military ID · A utility bill or a bank statement · Organization formation documents · Documents that confirm the Security Company's legitimacy · Trademark Notice · DMCA Takedown Notice · HMRC tax notification · A screenshot of the PayPal transaction details · Court orders · Birth Certificate · Death Certificate · Change of name certificate · Marriage license.

Do the arithmetic on that list, because the headline is misleading:

- **6 of 18 (33.3%)** are the photo IDs people mean when they say "KYC" — passport, identity card, permanent resident card, health insurance card with photo, driver's license, U.S. Military ID.
- **10 of 18 (55.6%)** are government or civil-status records (the 6 above plus birth certificate, death certificate, change of name certificate, marriage license).
- **8 of 18 (44.4%)** are not identity documents at all — a utility bill or bank statement, company formation documents, security-company legitimacy documents, a trademark notice, a DMCA takedown notice, an HMRC tax notification, a PayPal transaction screenshot, and court orders.
- The list is self-declared incomplete: "The list of the documents is not complete, and in some cases, we may request providing or filling out additional documents and request their notarization." **Notarisation** is on the table.

The mechanics are more specific than any other host's. Verification runs through **Veriff**, and the walkthrough asks for **three images**: "the client is asked to rake the photos of both ID sides and selfie". The trigger is an email "containing a Veriff link from the Risk Management department" — note that it is *Risk Management*, not Support — and the clock is hard:

> "**Q**: I have not submitted the details yet, but the link does not work. **A**: Please note that the link is valid for 7 days only."

**7 days** is the only published deadline in this entire comparison. Namecheap also splits the world into **11** country groups by which documents Veriff accepts; **1 of those 11** gets all four document types (passport, ID card, driver's licence, residence permit), and **1 of 11** — "New Zealand (Tokelau)" — is listed under "No documents supported". If you live in that second bucket, the published process has no path for you.

## Hostinger: discretionary ID, and a card photo that exposes 62.5% of your number

Hostinger's Universal Terms of Service does not make ID mandatory. It reserves the option:

> "If Hostinger has reason to believe that your Account information or any other information you provide to Hostinger is inaccurate, outdated, incomplete or unjustified, Hostinger reserves the right, in its sole and absolute discretion, to request you to validate the information (including to provide required supporting documents, which might include government-issued business identification or government-issued photo identification), to suspend or terminate your Account."

Two document classes are named (**government-issued business identification**, **government-issued photo identification**), the trigger is "reason to believe" — i.e. Hostinger's sole discretion, not a published rule — and the stated consequence of not complying is suspension or termination.

The second, much more specific trigger is a **chargeback**. From the refund policy:

> "Your use of the Hostinger Services and the ability to checkout using credit card will not resume until you: verify the payment method used for the disputed transaction, either by providing: proof of the payment; or a simple censored photo of the credit card, with uncovered first 6 (six) and last 4 (four) digits."

Run the numbers on that instruction. On a standard 16-digit card number, first 6 + last 4 = **10 of 16 digits uncovered (62.5%)**, with the middle **6 digits (37.5%)** hidden. That is the standard card-brand disclosure pattern — the first 6 are the BIN, the last 4 are the ones merchants are permitted to show — but it is worth knowing that "censored" here means "10 of 16 digits still legible", and that the penalty for not sending it is a **standing lock on credit-card checkout**, not just on the disputed order.

## DigitalOcean: no ID, but it verifies your instrument for up to $25.00

Search DigitalOcean's Terms of Service for a government-ID requirement and you get **zero** hits. What it does require, at §1.3, is "your name, email address, and a valid form of payment", and at §1.2, that you are "18 years of age or older" (or have equivalent legal capacity). §6.2 requires that information be "current, complete and accurate".

The surprising clause is §6.3:

> "You may also be billed an amount up to your current balance at any time to verify the accuracy of your account information."

So DigitalOcean's verification mechanism is a **charge against your own balance**, capped at that balance, at any time. Nothing in the ToS ties it to an identity document.

What DigitalOcean does verify, in detail, is the **payment instrument** — and it prices that verification differently per rail. From the payment-methods doc:

| Method | Verification charge | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Credit card | Preauthorisation request; "may appear on your statement for up to 7 days", no funds transferred | up to 7 days |
| PayPal | **$5** authorisation | — |
| Google Pay | **$0** | Chromium-based browsers only |
| Apple Pay | **$0** | Safari only |
| Alipay | **$0** | — |
| Crypto | **$25.00** one-time, "applied as a credit against your future service charges" | — |
| Bank account (ACH) | Two micro-deposits; you must confirm "within ten days" | 2 micro-deposits / 10 days |

Measured against DigitalOcean's cheapest Droplet — **$4.00/mo, $0.00595/hr** for `s-1vcpu-512mb-10gb`, read off the pricing page on 2026-10-16 — that ladder is **0.00 months** of server time at $0, **1.25 months** at $5.00, and **6.25 months** at $25.00. The spread between the cheapest and the most expensive way to prove you are a real payment method is **$25.00**, and the two $0 rails are gated on **which browser you are using**.

## Liquid Web: creditworthiness, not identity

Liquid Web's Terms of Service contains no identity-verification requirement for opening an account. The closest provision replaces identity with credit:

> "Delivery of the Services is subject to the continuing approval of your creditworthiness. You shall furnish financial information as we may reasonably request to determine your creditworthiness."

Its privacy policy lists what it collects to create an account: "your name, email address, physical address, phone number, credit card information, and website domain" — **six** fields, and unlike Hetzner, where the phone number is optional and tied to "advanced verification", here it is in the baseline set.

The identity verification that Liquid Web *does* publish is for privacy-rights requests, not hosting, and it carries the only real clocks in its policy: a response "within **45 days**", an appeal window of "**30 days**", and a decision on appeal within "**60 days**". For hosting, the lever is refusal, not verification: "We reserve the right to refuse to provide you with our Services in our sole discretion and without notice."

## What the three big comparison sites actually show you

Checked on 2026-10-16, none of the three answer this question on the first screen:

- **LowEndBox** — the homepage is a stream of teasers. Provider, region, RAM and price appear only inside the headline text; the structured fields are author, date and comment count. There is no mention of identity verification, KYC, ID documents, passports or account approval anywhere on the page. "VPN" appears, but only as a navigation tag under Specializations — the exact opposite of Hetzner's advice, which is that a VPN will get you flagged.
- **Namecheap** — the homepage shows no VPS card at all; VPS is a navigation link only. Domain, email and shared-hosting cards are priced and show renewal figures, and identity verification appears nowhere. The only "validation" language on the page is **SSL certificate types in the footer** — "Domain Validation", "Organization Validation", "Extended Validation" — which are certificate-assurance levels, not account checks, and are routinely mistaken for KYC.
- **Liquid Web** — the packages page lists 8 GB at $150.30/mo (renews at $2,004/year), 16 GB at $175.50/mo (renews at $2,676/year) and 32 GB at $256.50/mo (renews at $5,280/year). There is no mention of verification, ID, or account approval. The only occurrence of "ID" on the page is inside "Dedicated IP address".

So the page that would tell you whether your cheap VPS deal needs a passport does not exist on any of the three. You have to read the host's own legal and support pages, which is what this article did.

## What we could not verify (2026-10-16, no proxies, no UA changes)

- **Liquid Web** — `liquidweb.com/policies/*` returns **403** to our automated fetcher; the quotes above were read from the publicly accessible page. No identity-verification requirement for hosting was found in either policy.
- **Hetzner** — no minimum amount is published for the prepayment verification path, and no deadline is published for responding to a verification request. Both are **not verifiable**; we did not estimate them.
- **Hostinger** — no deadline is published for responding to a validation request, and the refund policy does not state how long the credit-card checkout lock lasts. **Not verifiable.**
- **Vultr** — 403 on this run. Not included.
- **Hetzner's Server Auction and Cloud pricing** — client-rendered; no prices captured, so no price-based arithmetic is asserted for Hetzner anywhere above.

## What to do before you buy, in five minutes

1. **Decide what you are willing to hand over before you hit checkout.** If the answer is "nothing", your realistic shortlist is DigitalOcean (instrument verification, $0 on Google Pay / Apple Pay / Alipay) and Liquid Web (credit check) — not the $3.88/mo end of the market.
2. **If you are going with Hetzner, do not register over a VPN and do not use a throwaway free email address.** Both are named in its own fraud-prevention FAQ as things that make verification harder. Make your first order small; its FAQ says large first-time orders are the ones that get rejected.
3. **If you are going with Hetzner and choose prepayment over the ID, treat that money as locked.** It is only refundable when you fully close the account with no outstanding invoices, and Hetzner issues no invoice for it.
4. **If Namecheap flags you, you have 7 days.** The link comes from the Risk Management department and dies after a week; you will need the ID, both sides, plus a selfie. Check in advance whether your country is in the "No documents supported" group.
5. **Never email an ID.** Namecheap states it "will **never** request you to send your private information as an email attachment" and that government ID is collected only through Veriff. Any email asking otherwise is the phishing attempt, not the check.
6. **On Hostinger, avoid the chargeback route entirely.** A chargeback does not just cost you the dispute — it locks credit-card checkout until you send a card photo showing 10 of 16 digits.
7. **Do not assume "no ID at signup" means "no check ever".** Hetzner verifies before processing an *order*, Hostinger verifies on "reason to believe", and DigitalOcean's ToS §6.3 permits a balance-sized charge at any time. Registration is not approval.

articles.title: Cheap VPS Deals: How Many Days You Get After a Payment Fails — Before the VPS Is Switched Off and Deleted
articles.description: Read off the hosts' own pages on 2026-10-17: only one of five publishes a real deadline. Namecheap cancels a VPS exactly 7 days after the billing date — suspension and cancellation on the same day, with retries on day 2 and day 5. Hetzner gives you 10 days to pay, then up to 4 reminders, and its last remaining payment rail (bank transfer, 'up to two weeks' to arrive) is slower than the deadline it cures. Hostinger's grace period is not a number: it is whatever is left of your subscription period, 0 to 30 days. Liquid Web's is 10 days plus a 1.5%/month late charge, and stopping payment on day 1 of an annual VPS can turn a $150.30 invoice into a $1,653.30 early-termination claim — 11.0x. DigitalOcean publishes no timeline at all, and 'past due' does not stop your server.
articles.question: If my card fails on a cheap VPS deal, how many days do I have before the host suspends the server, and how many before it deletes it?
articles.body:
**Read off five hosts' own pages on 2026-10-17: exactly one of them publishes a date you can put in a calendar. Namecheap says a VPS is "suspended and cancelled 7 days later" than the billing date — and it does both on the same day, so there is no window in which your server is merely switched off. Hetzner says invoices are payable "within ten days." Hostinger publishes no grace period at all: it retries your card "until the current subscription period ends," which is a number between 30 and 0 depending on where in the month it tried. Liquid Web gives a 10-day cure period after written notice and charges 1.5% per month on the unpaid balance. DigitalOcean states plainly that it "does not publish fixed timelines for these stages."**

The second thing nobody tells you is that **"past due" is not "switched off."** DigitalOcean's own late-payment page says that when an account is past due, "The account's existing resources continue to run" — what stops is your ability to create new ones. The power-off happens one stage later, at *suspended*. If you are watching for your VPS to go dark as the warning sign, you are watching for the wrong event, and by then you have already lost one stage.

This matters more on cheap VPS deals than anywhere else, because the cheap end of the market is where annual prepay, expiring cards and $4/month auto-charges collide. Below is every number these five hosts actually publish, plus the arithmetic that turns them into deadlines.

## The runway table — copy this, it is the whole article

Runway is measured from the moment money is first demanded to the moment the server is unrecoverable. `L` = days between invoice issuance and the due date; `C` = days you get after the due date.

| Host | Invoice sent (`L`) | Due / grace after due (`C`) | Total published runway | Switched off and deleted on the same day? | Recoverable after? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Namecheap** (VPS) | 7 days before billing date | **7 days** | **14 days** | **Yes** — "suspended and cancelled 7 days later" | Often yes (see below) |
| **Hetzner** | 0 (due immediately) | **10 days** | 10 days + up to 4 reminders | No, staged: lock → cancel → delete | Only if paid before the termination notice |
| **Hostinger** | 0–30 days before period end | Remainder of the subscription period | **0–30 days** | Yes — "terminate upon expiration" | Not stated |
| **Liquid Web** | Not stated | **10 days** after written notice (nonpayment) | ≥10 days | No — 15 days from notice before a suspension becomes termination | Not stated |
| **DigitalOcean** | 0 (billed on the 1st for prior month) | **Not published** | **Unknown** | No — 3 distinct stages | **No** — "Deleted resources cannot be recovered" |

Only Namecheap gives you a number and a second number. Everyone else gives you a stage list and a discretion clause.

## Namecheap: the only host that tells you the exact day

Namecheap's *Invoicing policies* article (last updated 6/9/2026) is the single most specific document any of these five hosts publishes about non-payment. The timeline, in the order the page gives it:

1. **Billing date − 7 days** — "Hosting accounts are invoiced 7 days prior to billing date. An invoice notification email is sent out at the time of invoice generation indicating the outstanding amount and the due date."
2. **Billing date** — "Invoices are due on the billing date." With auto-renewal on, the card is charged "on the 7th day after invoice generation (i.e., on the billing date)."
3. **Billing date + 2 and + 5 days** — "In case the first auto-renewal attempt failed, the system will try to renew the hosting plan on the 2 and 5 days after the billing date."
4. **Billing date + 7 days** — "If the outstanding invoice remains unpaid after the billing date, your hosting account will be suspended and cancelled 7 days later (for Shared packages, VPS and Dedicated server) and 23 days later (for Reseller packages)."

Two things fall out of that which no deal roundup ever mentions.

**The last retry and the cancellation are two days apart, not seven.** The retry schedule compresses: attempts land on D+0, D+2 and D+5, and the axe falls at D+7. So after the *final* automatic charge attempt you have **2 days**, not 7.

**An expired card is treated worse than a declined one.** The page continues: "If the system receives an error related to invalidity of a card (i.e. the attached card expired) it sets a pause in 7 days till the next charge. Thus, there will be only one more automatic attempt to renew the service before it is suspended." A 7-day pause starting from the billing date lands the final attempt on the same day the 7-day suspension clock expires — and the page says that attempt is the last one before suspension. **A hard card failure and a soft card failure do not get the same runway.**

Namecheap also publishes how cancellation is priced differently per product. Subscription-based dedicated servers are "cancelled in 3 days after the billing date" if auto-renewal is on, and **on the billing date itself** if it is off. A VPS gets 7 days: **2.33x the runway of a subscription dedicated server with auto-renewal enabled, and infinitely more than one without it.**

On recovery, Namecheap is the most forgiving of the five, and it publishes the price. Its reactivation article (updated 5/9/2025) says VPS "backups are generated once a week, during the weekend, for all VPS Packages, regardless of the management type," and "backups are over-written by newly created ones." That gives a hard bound on the damage: **your worst-case data loss is the writes since the previous weekend — up to 7 days.** Three further costs are stated in the same article:

- After restoration, "your VPS will have a new IP address." Your DNS and any IP allowlists break, and that is not optional.
- If you only want the data and not a restored server: "You'll need to add $15 to your Namecheap funds."
- VPS Complete Management gets 100 GB of backup storage and backups "3 times a week"; extra space is "$10 per 10 GB of additional backup disk space" — **$1.00/GB**.

The dedicated-server line in the same article is the one to read before you buy anything bigger: "After your dedicated server is canceled, all data is deleted from the server. It is impossible to obtain a backup for User-Responsible servers or servers with the Basic Management option."

## Hetzner: 10 days, four reminders, and a payment rail slower than the deadline

Hetzner's payment overview (last changed 2026-07-28) is blunt: "Invoices are due immediately. You must pay within ten days for all your invoices. After that, we will send you an email reminder." Its data-protection FAQ (last changed 2026-07-20) adds the count: "we will send a total of four payment reminders. In the third payment reminder, we will inform you that your account will be deactivated if payment is still not received."

So the warning arrives in reminder 3 of 4 — **you get exactly one more notice after being told the account will be deactivated.**

What happens next is a menu, not a schedule. The payment overview lists three possible steps — "Lock one or more of your Hetzner servers or services," "Cancel your Hetzner products," "Lock or delete your entire Hetzner account" — and then: "We make decisions about this on a case-by-case basis." New accounts are explicitly faster: "For new accounts, we usually react more quickly to late payments... If you do not pay your first invoice within a short period of time, we may lock your Hetzner servers and other products at an early stage." **A first invoice is treated differently from a twentieth invoice.**

Then comes the trap. As an invoice gets later, Hetzner removes payment methods: "If your late payment is later or very late, we may deactivate these options to help prevent abuse and fraud. If your invoice is very late, we will only accept payment via a bank/wire transfer." And bank transfers, per the same page, take **"up to two weeks"** to arrive.

That is a 14-day settlement time on a 10-day deadline — **the only rail left is 1.4x slower than the clock it is supposed to stop.** If you intend to cure a Hetzner late payment by wire, you are already late by construction.

There is also a hard, non-appealable cliff that no other host here states as plainly: "We will reactivate your account automatically once we process your payment. We will only do so if we receive the payment before we issue a notice of termination. **You cannot revoke a notice of termination that we issue.**"

And on data: "Your data may or may not still be available after we have locked or cancelled your Hetzner product or account. It depends on how late your invoice is and on your specific situation. We do not guarantee that you will be able to restore your data." Access returns only "after you have paid all late invoices, and after we have reactivated your Hetzner products and account." Failed charges on the automatic route may be retried "up to five times" before you have to ask billing to charge the card manually; unresolved debts go to "a debt collection agency," which "will result in additional fees that will increase the original invoice amount."

## Hostinger: the grace period is not a number

Hostinger's Universal Terms of Service §16 does not give a grace period, because structurally it cannot. Auto-renewal is charged at a Charge Date that is "from 30 (thirty) to 0 (zero) calendar days before the end of the current subscription period." Then: "If we cannot charge the renewal payment at the scheduled Charge Date, we may make additional attempts to charge your Payment Method(s) linked to your Account **until the current subscription period ends**."

**Your Hostinger grace period equals whatever is left of your subscription period — anywhere from 30 days down to 0**, decided by where in that 30-to-0 window Hostinger happened to schedule the charge. Two customers on identical plans can get wildly different runways, and neither is published.

Turn auto-renewal off and the number goes to zero explicitly: "should you disable the auto-renewal and fail to manually renew your Services before the end of the then-current subscription period, your Services will terminate upon expiration of the then-current subscription period." Note that this is the *only* one of the five where switching off auto-renewal — the thing everyone is told to do to avoid renewal shock — is also the thing that removes your grace period entirely.

Three more clauses decide what a non-payment actually costs you at Hostinger:

- **No money back once it stops.** "All fees for Services are non-refundable (even if your Services are suspended, terminated or restricted in any other manner, or transferred prior to the end of the Services' subscription period)."
- **A chargeback skips the whole ladder.** On receiving "notification of a chargeback, reversal, payment dispute, or is charged a penalty," Hostinger may pursue "immediate cancellation, termination or suspension, **without notice to you**." No Charge Date, no retries, no remainder of the period.
- **Destruction is discretionary and includes backups.** Where restrictions are applied, Hostinger "may, in its sole and absolute discretion, remove and destroy any data and files (**including back-up copies**) stored by you on its servers, and has no obligation to provide you with such data and files."

Hostinger also disclaims the outcome outright: "Hostinger is not responsible for the loss of Services resulting from an inability to collect fees for Services from your Payment Method(s)." And any balance you were holding is not a rescue fund — credits "will expire after 2 (two) years from their issuance," may be applied by Hostinger to "any outstanding fees (including for the purpose of charging auto-renewal payment)," and "In the event that your Account is terminated... any remaining available credits in Hostinger Balance will be forfeited."

## Liquid Web: 10 days to cure, then 11.0x the invoice

Liquid Web's Terms of Service (effective May 8, 2024) is the only document here with a **price** attached to being late: "we may impose a late charge in an amount equal to one and one-half percent (1½%)... of the unpaid balance per month." On its entry VPS package — 8 GB, 4 vCPU, 240 GB, 5 TB at **$150.30/mo**, renewing at $2,004/year — that is **$2.25 per month** on the unpaid balance.

The timing is in §8. Either party may terminate on written notice if the other defaults and the default "continues for a period of thirty (30) days after receipt of written notice specifying the nature of the breach, or a period of **ten (10) days** in the case of nonpayment of Fees." Nonpayment gets a third of the cure period of any other breach. Separately, breach-based suspensions convert: "In the event you are unable to cure the breach within fifteen (15) days of our notice, the suspension may be treated as a termination for cause."

Two clocks, two different triggers, and the page never says they cannot both run — **≥10 days for nonpayment, plus up to 15 more before a suspension hardens into a termination.**

The number that should stop you is the early-termination charge. Nonpayment "resulting in the termination of the Agreement... shall entitle us to collect from you... one hundred percent (100%) of the monthly recurring charges for the Services multiplied by the number of months remaining in the Service Term," payable "within sixty (60) days of termination."

Run that on the published prices. Stop paying on the entry package one month into a 12-month term and 11 months remain:

| Package | Monthly | Months remaining | Early-termination charge | Multiple of the one unpaid invoice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 GB | $150.30 | 11 | **$1,653.30** | **11.0x** |
| 16 GB | $175.50 | 11 | **$1,930.50** | **11.0x** |
| 32 GB | $256.50 | 11 | **$2,821.50** | **11.0x** |

**A single failed $150.30 payment on day one becomes a $1,653.30 claim — exactly 11.0x the invoice you missed**, on a service you no longer have. (Assumes the "monthly recurring charges" are the introductory monthly rates printed on the packages page; the ToS does not specify which rate applies.)

Two more from the same document: "During the suspension period, we shall have the right to deny access to, and/or, destroy data stored on the compromised server or account," and on data generally, "You shall be responsible for maintaining all backups of all Customer Data on our servers." You also have "thirty (30) days" to dispute a charge — **three times the cure period for not paying it.**

## DigitalOcean: three stages, zero days

DigitalOcean's late-payments page (last updated 2026-07-15) is the clearest description of the *shape* of the process and the only one that refuses to quantify it. The three stages, verbatim:

- **Past due:** "We email the account owner. We place the account on hold, which prevents creating new resources. **The account's existing resources continue to run.** In certain cases, any Spaces on the account cannot be accessed."
- **Suspended:** "We power down the account's resources. We redirect logins to the payment page."
- **Permanently deleted:** "If an unresolved balance continues after suspension, we may permanently delete the account's resources. **Deleted resources cannot be recovered.** The account owner can still pay the balance to access the account, but they must recreate any resources that were removed."

And then, in the page's own words: "How fast an account moves between past due, suspension, and permanent deletion depends on the account. **DigitalOcean does not publish fixed timelines for these stages.**"

So the honest answer for DigitalOcean is: **nobody outside DigitalOcean knows, and DigitalOcean says so.** That is a better answer than the fake "30 days" that gets repeated on forums, and it is the reason this article exists.

Two operational details cost people real downtime. First, **paying does not bring the server back**: "After your account is current, you must manually power on Droplets that were powered off. **We do not automatically power on any resources for you.**" There are two clocks at DigitalOcean — the money clock and the downtime clock — and only one of them stops when you pay. Second, there is no escape valve: "We do not offer refunds" and "We do not offer extensions."

Here is the arithmetic that explains why cheap DigitalOcean setups almost never see the mid-month enforcement event at all. DigitalOcean may "charge your primary payment method earlier in the month when your outstanding balance reaches your tier's auto-charge amount," and the tier table (last updated 2026-09-30) starts at **$25** for Tier 1. The cheapest Basic Droplet on the pricing page today (2026-10-17) is 512 MiB / 1 vCPU / 10 GiB SSD at **$0.00595/hr, $4.00/mo**. $25 ÷ $4.00 = **6.25**, so:

| Tier | Auto-charge amount | Cheapest Droplets needed to reach it in a month |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 | $25 | **7** (6 × $4.00 = $24.00 is under; 7 × $4.00 = $28.00 is over) |
| Tier 2 | $50 | **13** |
| Tier 3 | $250 | **63** |
| Tier 4 | $1,000 | **250** |
| Tier 5 | $4,000 | **1,000** |

**You need seven entry Droplets running before DigitalOcean's mid-month charge can even fire.** For the one-Droplet buyer — the entire audience of a cheap VPS deal — the only enforcement event that exists is the invoice on the first of the month, which means the whole past-due → suspended → deleted ladder can only start on the 1st.

## What the three big comparison sites show instead

Read on 2026-10-17, all three of the sites that rank for `vps deals` are silent on this.

- **LowEndBox** — the homepage is a directory and post feed. Every card carries exactly six fields: title, author, date, comment count, excerpt, and a "Read More" link. Price, RAM and location exist only inside free-text headlines. The words *non-payment*, *overdue*, *invoice*, *grace period*, *suspend* and *deleted* appear **nowhere** on the page.
- **Namecheap** — the homepage has **no VPS card at all**; VPS is a navigation link only. The product cards that are present all print renewal figures (`.com` "renews at $18.48/year", Private Email "Renews at $41.88/year"), so the mechanism exists — it is simply never applied to VPS, and there is no non-payment language anywhere on the page.
- **Liquid Web** — the VPS packages page gives three tiers ($150.30 / $175.50 / $256.50 per month, renewing at $2,004 / $2,676 / $5,280 per year, 10% / 21% / 42% off) plus a four-question FAQ covering what a VPS package is and what to do if you outgrow one. **Zero non-payment, suspension or deletion content**, and no billing FAQ.

The pattern is consistent with the earlier gaps in this series: these pages are built to rank for *what a deal costs*, never for *what happens when the deal stops being paid for*. That is precisely why the numbers above had to be dug out of billing docs, KB articles and terms of service.

## Not verifiable today (2026-10-17)

Stated plainly rather than filled in from memory or proxies:

- **Vultr** — `vultr.com/pricing` returned **403** to direct access; no timeline obtained.
- **Namecheap VPS product page** — `namecheap.com/hosting/vps/` returned **403** to direct script access. Everything Namecheap above comes from its **publicly readable Knowledgebase**, which is a different path and was reachable.
- **Liquid Web** — `liquidweb.com/vps-hosting/packages/` returned **403** to direct script access; the package prices and the Terms of Service clauses were read from the public pages and are labelled as such.
- **Hetzner Cloud pricing** — server prices are client-side rendered and could not be read, so **no Hetzner price arithmetic is asserted anywhere in this article**, only its published day counts.
- **DigitalOcean** — the number of days between stages is not published. That is a fact about the host, not a gap in this research.
- **Hostinger** — no published number of retry attempts, and no published notice period before termination.

## What to do with this

1. **Put the Namecheap date in your calendar if you use Namecheap.** Billing date + 7 is the day the VPS is both suspended and cancelled. Do not wait for the D+5 retry to fail.
2. **Assume DigitalOcean's clock is shorter than you think, because it is unpublished.** Treat the "past due" email as your only warning — by the "suspended" email your Droplets are already powered down.
3. **After paying DigitalOcean, power the Droplets back on yourself.** "We do not automatically power on any resources for you" is the entire difference between a one-hour outage and a multi-day one.
4. **Do not plan to cure a Hetzner default by wire transfer.** "Up to two weeks" to arrive against a 10-day due date means the rail outlives the deadline. Keep a card or SEPA mandate valid on the account.
5. **If you use Hostinger and turn off auto-renewal, you have also turned off your grace period.** Services "terminate upon expiration" — re-add a valid card rather than relying on the remainder of the term.
6. **Never let a Liquid Web annual VPS go unpaid in month one.** 11 months × $150.30 = $1,653.30, due within 60 days, for a service you no longer have.
7. **Backups are the only thing that survives every one of these five policies.** Namecheap's own VPS backups are weekly and overwritten, so worst case you lose a week; Hetzner and DigitalOcean both explicitly do not guarantee your data survives. Namecheap charges **$15** for data-only retrieval — cheap relative to every alternative on this page.

articles.title: Cheap VPS Deals: What Each Host Will Actually Take as Payment — and What Crypto Costs You
articles.description: Read off providers' own pages on 2026-10-15: DigitalOcean takes 7 card brands plus PayPal/Google Pay/Apple Pay/Alipay/Link plus stablecoins from 400+ wallets, and charges $25.00 to verify a crypto wallet but $0 to verify Apple Pay. Hetzner takes 4 card brands, SEPA (EUR accounts only), wire and PayPal, and states plainly 'We do not accept cryptocurrencies.' Hostinger accepts crypto and then says crypto purchases 'will not be refunded.' Namecheap and Liquid Web publish no payment-method list at all.
articles.question: Can I pay for a cheap VPS deal with PayPal or crypto, and can I get that money back if I change my mind?
articles.body:
**Read off the providers' own billing pages on 2026-10-15, the answer is that the cheap-VPS market has no shared payment baseline: DigitalOcean takes 7 card brands, 5 third-party wallets and stablecoins from "over 400 wallets"; Hetzner takes 4 card brands, SEPA for EUR accounts only, wire transfer and PayPal — and writes "We do not accept cryptocurrencies"; Hostinger takes crypto and then writes that crypto purchases "will not be refunded." Namecheap and Liquid Web publish no payment-method list on their VPS pages at all.** The payment rail you pick is not a neutral checkout choice. On these three hosts it decides whether you can get a refund, how long your money is in transit, and in one case which browser you are allowed to use.

## The matrix, read off official pages on 2026-10-15

| Rail | DigitalOcean | Hetzner | Hostinger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Card brands | Visa, MasterCard, Amex, Discover, UnionPay, Diners Club, JCB (**7**) | VISA, Mastercard, AMEX, UnionPay (**4**) | Not enumerated on the VPS page; ToS refers to "valid and eligible payment methods specified here" |
| Debit cards | Yes | Not listed separately | Not enumerated |
| SEPA direct debit | No | **Yes — EUR accounts only** | Not verifiable |
| US ACH direct debit | **Yes — qualifying customers, U.S. banks** | No | No |
| Bank / wire transfer | No | Yes (manual) | Not verifiable |
| PayPal | Yes | Yes — **manual payment only** | Not enumerated |
| Google Pay | Yes (Chromium browsers only) | Not listed | Not verifiable |
| Apple Pay | Yes (Safari only) | **No — "even if they are linked to a credit card"** | Not verifiable |
| Alipay | Yes | Not listed | Not verifiable |
| Link | Yes | Not listed | Not verifiable |
| Crypto | **Yes — stablecoins, 400+ wallets, limited availability** | **No — "We do not accept cryptocurrencies."** | **Yes** |
| Explicitly rejected | Virtual, electron and prepaid cards | Apple Pay, crypto, partial payments and payment plans | Not enumerated |

Two things fall out of that grid immediately. First, **there is no method all three accept** except ordinary credit cards — and even there the brand lists differ: Discover, Diners Club and JCB work at DigitalOcean and appear nowhere in Hetzner's list. Second, **the two direct-debit rails are mutually exclusive by geography**: Hetzner's SEPA is "only available for EUR accounts," DigitalOcean's ACH is for "qualifying customers with U.S. bank accounts." A euro-zone customer and a US customer are looking at two completely different automatic-debit options on two different hosts.

## Crypto: three hosts, three incompatible policies

This is the part that actually costs money, and the three majors do not agree on it at all.

**Hetzner refuses it outright.** Its [Payment Overview](https://docs.hetzner.com/general/billing-and-account-management/billing-at-hetzner/payment-overview/) (last changed 2026-07-28, article ID GE-CE966) states: *"We do not accept cryptocurrencies."* Its terms and conditions go further on the compute side — *"The operation of applications for mining cryptocurrencies remains prohibited."*

**Hostinger accepts it and removes the exit.** The [Hostinger Refund Policy](https://www.hostinger.com/legal/refund-policy) says:

> Due to their nature, cryptocurrencies, tokens and digital assets are generally irreversible and their exchange rates are highly volatile and transitory... **Products purchased using cryptocurrencies, tokens or digital assets will not be refunded.**

Note how that stacks with Hostinger's VPS-specific refund gate, which is already the strictest in the group: a VPS plan is refundable only if the request lands *"within 30 days from the date of the transaction"* **and** *"more than 180 days have passed from the moment of initiation of last refund for any other VPS hosting plan."* Pay with a card and you have one narrow, once-per-180-days window. Pay with crypto and you have no window at all — the 30-day policy exists, but the payment rail voids it.

**DigitalOcean accepts it and charges $25.00 to let you.** Per [Manage Payment Methods](https://docs.digitalocean.com/platform/billing/manage-payment-methods/): *"During setup we initiate a one-time authorization charge of $25.00. This payment is applied as a credit against your future service charges."* Access is *"currently limited and may not be available to all customers in all locations,"* and only stablecoins are supported.

Put that $25.00 next to DigitalOcean's own cheapest Droplet, read from the [pricing page](https://www.digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets) the same day: 512 MiB / 1 vCPU / 10 GiB / 500 GiB transfer at **$0.00595/hr and $4.00/mo**. The verification charge is therefore **6.25 months of that machine's list price** (25.00 ÷ 4.00 = 6.25). It is not refunded to you as cash — it is booked as credit, and DigitalOcean's refund answer is a flat *"We do not offer refunds."*

## The setup-price ladder nobody prints on the checkout page

DigitalOcean charges a different amount to verify each wallet type, and the spread is 5x:

| Method added | Authorization charge at setup | Source wording |
|---|---|---|
| Crypto wallet | **$25.00** | "one-time authorization charge of $25.00... applied as a credit against your future service charges" |
| PayPal | **$5** | "you choose a payment method from PayPal and allow a $5 authorization charge" |
| Google Pay | **$0** | "allow a $0 authorization charge" |
| Apple Pay | **$0** | "allow a $0 authorization charge" |
| Alipay | **$0** | "allow a $0 authorization charge" |
| Credit / debit card | no charge, but a hold | "temporary preauthorization holds may appear on your statement for up to 7 days" |

Crypto costs **5.0x** what PayPal costs to attach (25.00 ÷ 5 = 5.0), and PayPal costs infinitely more than the three $0 options. Against the $4.00/mo Droplet: the PayPal $5 is **1.25 months** of service, the crypto $25 is **6.25 months**. The prepayment is credited back, but the point stands — attaching a crypto wallet to a $4/month VPS deal means fronting more than half a year of that machine's price before the machine exists.

There is a neat coincidence worth knowing: **$25 is also DigitalOcean's Tier 1 auto-charge amount.** Per [How to Pay Your Bill](https://docs.digitalocean.com/platform/billing/pay-bills/), the tier table is:

| Tier | Prepayment amount | Auto-charge amount |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 | No Prepay | **$25** |
| Tier 2 | $50 | $50 |
| Tier 3 | $250 | $250 |
| Tier 4 | $1,000 | $1,000 |
| Tier 5 | $4,000 | $4,000 |

So a brand-new team is auto-charged the moment it owes $25 — which on that $4.00/mo Droplet is **6.25 months of usage** (25 ÷ 4.00), the same 6.25 ratio as the crypto verification charge. And climbing from Tier 1 to Tier 2 requires a **$50 prepayment = 12.5 months** of the same machine prepaid up front.

## Your browser decides which wallets you are offered

Two of DigitalOcean's five third-party rails are browser-gated, in writing:

- **Google Pay** — *"The Google Pay option only appears if you are using a Chromium-based browser, like Chrome, Brave, or Microsoft Edge."*
- **Apple Pay** — *"The Apple Pay option only appears if you are using the Safari browser."*

Neither statement leaves room for a third case. On a browser that is neither Chromium-based nor Safari — Firefox being the obvious one — the two wallet options the docs describe are simply not offered, which pushes you onto card, PayPal, Alipay, Link, crypto or ACH. Hetzner's version of this is a flat refusal rather than a browser rule: *"We do not accept other forms of payment, even if they are linked to a credit card (e.g. Apple Pay)."* So an Apple Pay user with a Visa behind it can pay DigitalOcean and cannot pay Hetzner.

## The ACH one-way door at DigitalOcean

Adding a US bank account is not symmetric with adding a card. Per the same page:

> Once you add a bank account, ACH direct debit becomes the default payment method on your team. **To change the default payment method, you need to remove the bank account as a payment method.**

And separately: *"You cannot remove the default payment method on the team."* Read together, those two lines mean the bank account **seizes** the default slot, and the only way to give it back to your card is to delete the bank account entirely. Verification is not instant either — manual entry triggers *"two small micro-deposits"* that you must confirm *"within ten days."*

Speed differs by rail in a way that matters if you are restoring a suspended machine. DigitalOcean: card and third-party payments post quickly, but *"When using PayPal, your balance updates after your payment is processed, which often takes several hours"* and *"PayPal also sometimes holds payments for up to 72 hours."* ACH is slowest — *"which can take several business days."* Its own support doc adds that after you clear a past-due balance you *"need to manually turn your resources (like Droplets) back on"* — paying is not the same as being restored.

## Hostinger's refund outcome depends on which country's rail you used

Hostinger's refund policy splits payment methods into a four-level ladder, and the level is set by the rail, not by the product:

| Level | Payment methods | What you can get |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Cryptocurrencies, tokens, digital assets | **Nothing.** "will not be refunded" |
| 1 | Multibanco (Portugal), GCash (Philippines), Fawry (Egypt) | **Hostinger Balance only** — "products purchased using these payment methods can not be refunded to the original payment source" |
| 2 | VTC Pay (Vietnam) | **Full refunds only** |
| 3 | Everything else | Original funding source, or Hostinger Balance at Hostinger's discretion |

Level 1 is the one to internalise: a Portuguese customer paying by Multibanco and a Vietnamese customer paying by VTC Pay bought the same VPS under the same 30-day policy and have materially different exits. Level 3 also carries a catch — *"once a refund to Hostinger Balance is initiated for a selected invoice, it becomes irrevocable and cannot be refunded to a different source."*

Separately, a chargeback is treated as a breach with a specific reopening condition: Hostinger *"may"* terminate immediately, credit-card checkout is disabled, and service does not resume until you *"verify the payment method used for the disputed transaction"* by supplying *"a simple censored photo of the credit card, with uncovered first 6 (six) and last 4 (four) digits."*

## Hetzner runs a clock, not a card

Hetzner's model is invoice-first, and the [payment overview](https://docs.hetzner.com/general/billing-and-account-management/billing-at-hetzner/payment-overview/) gives hard numbers:

- *"You must pay within ten days for all your invoices. After that, we will send you an email reminder."*
- Automatic charging is *"a few days after we issue the invoice"* for SEPA and credit card; PayPal and wire are **manual**.
- A failed payment *"can be attempted... up to five times"* before you must ask billing to charge the card manually.
- As lateness grows the rails close: *"If your late payment is later or very late, we may deactivate these options... If your invoice is very late, we will only accept payment via a bank/wire transfer."*
- Very late invoices *"may"* go to *"a debt collection agency"* with *"additional fees that will increase the original invoice amount."*

Prepayment works the opposite way from DigitalOcean's. DigitalOcean: *"A one-time prepayment can increase your trust tier and unlock higher limits immediately."* Hetzner: *"We don't provide an invoice for credit top-ups (prepayment). Invoices are issued only after the service has been provided"*, and credit balances are paid out *"only after the account has been fully closed and there are no outstanding invoices."* If prepaying to raise limits is your plan, only one of the two supports it.

## What the three benchmark sites give you: nothing

Checked on 2026-10-15, above the fold:

- **LowEndBox** — the homepage is a region/virtualization/specialization directory plus a post stream. Deal cards carry provider, region, virtualization, RAM, price, term, author, date and comment count. **Zero payment-method text anywhere on the first screen.** The closest thing is a coupon-code mention inside a headline.
- **Namecheap** — the VPS card reads *"From $3.88 Annual plan / Instead of $4.88/mo"* with a 20% badge. Adjacent non-VPS cards print renewal prices ($1.24, $9.88, $7.88, $3.88, $8.88). **No payment-method list on the VPS page.** The plan table does show *"30-day money-back guarantee"* on all five plans, which is a refund fact, not a payment fact.
- **Liquid Web** — three packages at $150.30 / $175.50 / $256.50 per month, renewing at $2,004 / $2,676 / $5,280 per year. Feature lists include "Unlimited inbound" and "Dedicated IP address." **No payment-method text anywhere on the page.**

All three are deal directories and checkout funnels. None answers "what can I pay with, and can I get it back" — which is exactly why that question is worth answering here.

## Not verifiable today

Stated rather than filled in. No proxy, no cache, no alternate user agent was used to read any of these:

- **Namecheap** — its payment-method list is not on the VPS page, and its legal and KB paths returned 403 to a direct request. The 30-day guarantee quoted above is from the readable VPS plan table; the accepted-payment list is **not verifiable**.
- **Liquid Web** — the packages page is readable but carries no payment-method text, and its legal paths returned 403. **Not verifiable.**
- **Vultr** — pricing and legal paths returned 403. **Not verifiable.**
- **Hostinger's full accepted-method list** — the ToS points to methods *"specified here"* via a link not resolvable in the fetched document, so the per-rail refund ladder above (which is complete and quoted) is used instead of an invented brand list.
- **DigitalOcean crypto availability** — the docs state access is *"currently limited and may not be available to all customers in all locations"*; no eligibility rule is published, so whether your account sees the option is **not verifiable** from documentation.

## What to do with this

1. **If you want a refund path, do not pay with crypto.** Hostinger cancels it outright, Hetzner does not accept it, and DigitalOcean's own refund answer is *"We do not offer refunds"* — so the $25.00 crypto verification charge is credit you must spend, not money you can retrieve.
2. **Check the brand before you blame the card.** Discover, Diners Club and JCB work at DigitalOcean and are absent from Hetzner's list; prepaid, virtual and electron cards are rejected at DigitalOcean by name.
3. **Match the debit rail to your currency.** SEPA is EUR-accounts-only at Hetzner; ACH is US-banks-only at DigitalOcean. Neither host offers the other's rail.
4. **Do not add a US bank account to DigitalOcean casually.** It becomes the default automatically, the default cannot be deleted, and reverting means removing the bank account and re-verifying by micro-deposit within ten days.
5. **Budget for settlement lag.** PayPal at DigitalOcean can be held *"up to 72 hours"*; ACH takes *"several business days"*; and paying a past-due DigitalOcean bill does not turn your Droplets back on by itself.
6. **If you pay at Hetzner, treat the invoice as a 10-day deadline with a 5-retry ceiling**, after which only a wire transfer is accepted and a collection agency becomes possible.
7. **If you are in Portugal, the Philippines, Egypt or Vietnam, read Hostinger's rail-specific table before you buy** — Multibanco, GCash and Fawry refund to balance only, VTC Pay refunds fully, and the difference is written into the policy.

Published 2026-10-15. Every figure above was read from the linked official pages on that date; where a host does not publish a number, this page says so instead of estimating one.

articles.title: Can You Send Email From a Cheap VPS Deal? Port 25, 465 and 587, Read off Providers' Own Docs
articles.description: Read on 2026-10-13: DigitalOcean blocks outbound SMTP ports 25, 465 AND 587 on every Droplet by default, including traffic through a Reserved IP. Hetzner blocks only 25 and 465, leaves 587 open, and will unblock on request after one month and your first paid invoice. The popular 'just use port 587' fix works on one of them and fails on the other.
articles.question: Can I send email from the VPS I'm about to buy, and which SMTP ports does the provider block by default?
articles.body:
**The short answer, taken from the providers' own documentation on 2026-10-13: on a DigitalOcean VPS you cannot send a single outbound SMTP message, because all three mail ports are blocked and no unblock path is published. On Hetzner you can send today — on port 587 only — and you can apply to have 25 and 465 opened after one month and your first paid invoice.** The two block lists differ by exactly one port, and it is the one every tutorial tells you to use instead.

DigitalOcean's support article *Why is SMTP blocked?* (last updated 2026-07-13) states it in one sentence:

> SMTP ports 25, 465, and 587 are blocked on Droplets to prevent spam and other abuses on our platform. This block applies to all Droplets by default and includes traffic passing through a Reserved IP address.

Hetzner's Cloud Servers FAQ, read the same day, says:

> That's why we block ports 25 and 465 by default on all cloud servers... Once you have been with us for a month and paid your first invoice, you can create a limit request to unblock these ports for a valid use case... As an alternative, you can also use port 587 to send emails via external mail delivery services. Port 587 is not blocked and can be used without sending a limit request.

| Outbound port | DigitalOcean Droplets | Hetzner Cloud Servers |
|---|---|---|
| 25 (SMTP, server-to-server) | **Blocked by default** | **Blocked by default** |
| 465 (SMTPS, implicit TLS) | **Blocked by default** | **Blocked by default** |
| 587 (submission) | **Blocked by default** | **Open** — usable with no limit request |
| Path to get 25/465 opened | None published; the doc recommends a third-party email provider instead | Limit request after **1 month + first paid invoice**; decided case-by-case |
| Scope of the rule | All Droplets, **including through a Reserved IP** | **Per account**; transferring a server to another account applies the new owner's rules |

## Why the "just use 587" advice breaks on one of them

Almost every "my VPS won't send mail" thread ends with *use port 587 instead of 25*. On Hetzner that is literally the vendor's own recommendation and it works with no permission. On DigitalOcean it cannot work, because 587 is inside the block list — switching ports moves you from one blocked port to another blocked port on the same host.

That leaves a DigitalOcean VPS with two ways out, both of which avoid SMTP entirely:

1. **Call an email API over HTTPS (443).** The block is on SMTP ports; the DigitalOcean doc's own recommendation is to use *"a third-party email as a service provider"*, and every provider below offers an HTTPS API alongside SMTP.
2. **Relay on a non-standard SMTP port.** Several relays accept submission on 2525. 2525 is not in DigitalOcean's published block list — but note carefully what that means: it is absent from the list, not guaranteed by it. Test before you depend on it.

## Test it yourself in 30 seconds, from inside the box

Run this on the VPS, not against it — the question is *outbound*, and an inbound port scan tells you nothing:

```bash
for p in 25 465 587 2525; do
  timeout 5 bash -c "cat < /dev/null > /dev/tcp/smtp.gmail.com/$p" \
    && echo "$p reachable" || echo "$p BLOCKED (no response in 5s)"
done
```

Reading the output: a TCP banner or `succeeded` means the path is open; a five-second hang that ends in failure is the signature of a provider-level filter. Two caveats before you blame the host: check your own `ufw`/`iptables` rules and the provider's cloud firewall first, because a self-inflicted DROP produces the identical timeout; and deliverability is a separate problem — an open port 25 gets your packets out, not into anyone's inbox.

## What sending actually costs instead

Running your own mail server is usually justified as the cheap option. The arithmetic says otherwise for almost everyone — and on DigitalOcean it is not available at any price.

DigitalOcean's cheapest Droplet (512 MB / 1 vCPU / 10 GiB / 500 GiB transfer) is **$4.00/mo at $0.00595/hr** on its pricing page. ($4.00 ÷ $0.00595 = 672.3, which is the same 672-hour monthly cap that shows up across its whole price list.) Amazon SES's pay-as-you-go rate is **$0.10 per 1,000 emails**.

> $4.00 ÷ ($0.10 ÷ 1,000) = **40,000 emails**

So one month of the cheapest possible VPS buys 40,000 delivered emails on SES. Below ~40,000 messages a month, renting the box costs more than not renting it — and the SES number is before you spend a single hour on postfix, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, or a blocklist appeal.

| Route | Official price read 2026-10-13 | Effective cost per 1,000 emails |
|---|---|---|
| Amazon SES, à la carte outbound | $0.10 / 1,000 | **$0.10** |
| Amazon SES, Essentials plan (0–10M/mo) | $0.16 / 1,000 | $0.16 |
| Resend Free | $0 — **3,000 emails/mo, 100/day**, 3 domains | $0 (capped) |
| Resend Pro | $20/mo — 50,000 emails/mo, then $0.90 / 1,000 | $0.40 at full quota |
| Resend Scale | $90/mo — 100,000 emails/mo, then $0.90 / 1,000 | $0.90 at full quota |
| Brevo Free | $0 — **300 emails/day** after account approval | $0 (capped) |
| Postmark Basic | $15/mo — 10,000 emails/mo, then $1.80 / 1,000 | $1.50 at plan floor |
| Postmark Pro | $16.50/mo — 10,000 emails/mo, then $1.30 / 1,000 | $1.65 at plan floor |

Three of those rows contain arithmetic worth doing before you pick a plan.

**SES's entry plan costs 60% more per email than paying à la carte.** $0.16 ÷ $0.10 = 1.60. If all you need is outbound sending, the à la carte rate wins; the plan exists for the bundled features (the Pro and Enterprise tiers also carry fixed monthly charges of $105 and $500 per account per region), not for a per-email discount.

**Resend's free tier is bound by a different limit depending on the month.** It allows 3,000 emails/mo *and* 100 emails/day. In a 31-day month the daily cap permits 3,100, so the monthly quota is what stops you at 3,000. In a 28-day February the daily cap permits only 2,800 — so **the daily limit is the binding one in short months and the monthly quota is the binding one in long months.** If your send pattern is spiky (1,000 invoices on the 1st), the daily cap is your real ceiling regardless.

**Brevo's free tier is 3x Resend's — with a gate.** 300 emails/day × 30 = 9,000/mo against Resend's 3,000/mo, a factor of 3.0. The condition is in Brevo's own FAQ wording: *"Once we approve your account for sending, you can start sending up to 300 emails per day."* Free volume you cannot start using the day you sign up is not the same as free volume you can.

**Postmark's Basic plan is cheaper per month and more expensive per extra email.** Basic is $15.00/mo with overages at $1.80/1,000; Pro is $16.50/mo with overages at $1.30/1,000. Solving for the crossover:

> 15.00 + 1.80x = 16.50 + 1.30x → 0.50x = 1.50 → x = 3 extra thousand

**Above 13,000 emails/month, Pro is the cheaper plan** even though its sticker price is 10% higher. Below that, Basic wins. The same logic applies to Resend Pro vs Scale: Scale costs $70/mo more for 50,000 extra emails, i.e. $1.40 per extra thousand, against an overage rate of $0.90 per thousand — so **stay on Pro and pay overages until you pass 50,000 + (70 ÷ 0.90) × 1,000 ≈ 127,800 emails/month**, at which point Scale is finally ahead.

## What we could not verify today, and why we did not fill it in

Under our own rules we do not bypass bot protection and we do not estimate unreadable numbers, so these are stated as unread rather than guessed:

- **Namecheap** — `namecheap.com` returned a Cloudflare interstitial (*"Just a moment..."*) to a direct request on 2026-10-13. No port policy read.
- **Liquid Web** — 403 to a direct request. Read via a normal page fetch: its VPS packages page shows 8 GB / 4 vCPU / 240 GB / 5 TB at $150.30/mo, 16 GB at $175.50/mo, 32 GB at $256.50/mo, with "Unlimited inbound" and "Dedicated IP address" in the feature list — and **zero mentions of email, SMTP or port 25 anywhere on the page**. The only place the word "inbound" appears is bandwidth.
- **Vultr** — 403 to `vultr.com/docs/` and to its docs article path.
- **Akamai / Linode** — `techdocs.akamai.com/linode/docs/send-email` returns a navigation shell with no body text, and its markdown endpoint 404s. No official statement extracted.
- **Hostinger** — its SMTP-settings help article redirects to a VPS DNS article; no port policy obtained.

For contrast, **LowEndBox**'s home page on 2026-10-13 carries provider, region, virtualization, RAM, price, term, author, date and comment count on its offer cards, and its filter taxonomy includes NVMe, DDoS and VPN — but no mail-related field at all. "email", "SMTP" and "port 25" appear nowhere on the page. A deal listing that never mentions outbound mail cannot tell you whether the box you are about to buy can send one.

## What to do, in order

1. **Decide whether you need port 25 at all.** If you are sending transactional mail (password resets, receipts, form notifications), you do not — use an HTTPS email API and the question disappears.
2. **If you are buying a DigitalOcean VPS, plan for zero outbound SMTP.** Ports 25, 465 and 587 are all blocked, including through a Reserved IP, and there is no published unblock request. Budget for a relay from day one; an API on 443 is the safe path.
3. **If you specifically need port 25, Hetzner is the realistic choice of the two** — but count the delay: one month plus your first paid invoice before you can even file the limit request, and then a case-by-case decision with no published SLA. Do not buy it for a mail launch next week.
4. **Run the four-port test above before you migrate anything**, and re-run it after changing cloud firewall rules.
5. **Price the relay against the box, not against zero.** At SES's $0.10/1,000, the cheapest Droplet's $4.00/mo is 40,000 emails — and that is before the maintenance you do not have to do.
6. **On Hetzner, remember the block follows the account, not the server.** Transfer a server to a project owned by another account and the new owner's port-blocking rules apply; check they have 25 and 465 unblocked *before* you move it.

articles.title: How Many Days Do You Actually Get to Change Your Mind on a VPS Deal?
articles.description: We read the refund terms on eight major VPS providers' own pages. Four publish a number, and it ranges from zero to 30 days. Four more hide theirs behind a bot wall. Here is the table, the exact wording, and how to use it before you buy.
articles.question: How many days do I have to get a refund on a VPS deal, and which providers actually publish a number?
articles.body:
The honest answer is that nobody will tell you, because four of the eight providers we checked **do not publish a verifiable refund window at all** — their own policy pages refuse automated readers, and one major provider's terms say the opposite of a guarantee. Of the four that do publish a number, the window runs from **zero days** to **30 days**. We pulled every quote below from the providers' own pages on 2026-10-09.

| Provider | Published window | What the page literally says |
|---|---|---|
| Hostinger | **30 days** | "may be refunded only if canceled within 30 days of the date of the transaction" |
| Namecheap | **30 days** | VPS page states "30-day money-back guarantee" |
| Hetzner | **14 days** | refund "at the latest fourteen days from the date of our receiving the notice of cancellation" |
| DigitalOcean | **None** | "any and all fees paid to us are non-refundable" |
| Liquid Web | No number | "Money-back guarantee varies based on product" |
| Vultr | Not verifiable | policy page returns a bot challenge |
| Linode (Akamai) | Not verifiable | policy page serves navigation only, no terms text |
| Contabo | Not verifiable | policy page returns a security check |

## Why the range is this wide

A refund window is not a customer-service perk. It is a legal position, and it tracks where the provider operates.

Hostinger's policy carries a revision stamp of **2026-10-02** — one week before we read it — which is the only page in this set that tells you how old its answer is. That matters more than the number itself: a refund policy you can date is a refund policy you can trust.

Hetzner's 14 days is a consumer withdrawal right under EU distance-selling rules, not a hosting-industry courtesy. Read the clause closely and you will see it is tied to *cancellation notice*, not to *purchase date*. The clock starts when they receive your notice, which means the practical deadline for you is earlier than 14 days after you buy.

DigitalOcean is the one that surprises people. Its terms of service do not offer a trial-and-refund path; they state fees are non-refundable. If you are comparing deals and you assume every host has a 30-day safety net, this is where that assumption costs you money.

## The part no comparison post tells you

Four of eight providers make their refund terms effectively unreadable to a machine. Vultr returns a Cloudflare challenge, Contabo returns a security check, Linode's policy route serves a navigation shell with no terms text, and Liquid Web answers with a sentence that manages expectations without committing to anything.

This is not a minor inconvenience, and it is not something the big comparison posts measure. If you cannot read a provider's refund terms before you buy, you are accepting a term you have not read — and the usual roundups quietly skip that, because a provider with no published number cannot be placed in a ranking table.

So treat it as a signal in itself. **A provider that makes its refund terms hard to read is telling you something about how hard the refund will be.**

## How to use this before you buy

Do not start the clock on the day the server feels slow. Start it on the day you pay.

1. **Write down the transaction date at checkout.** Hostinger's window runs from "the date of the transaction," not from provisioning, activation, or first login. On a deal where you prepay a year, that difference is the whole ballgame.
2. **Screenshot the plan card and the checkout total.** Every window here is contingent on *what* you bought. Liquid Web's own wording — "varies based on product" — is the industry telling you that the VPS line and the managed line on the same invoice can carry different terms.
3. **Set the reminder for day 25, not day 30.** Hetzner's 14 days runs from notice received, and cancellation notices need processing time. A reminder on the last day is a reminder that arrives too late.
4. **If the provider publishes no number, assume zero.** Not "assume 30." Zero. That is what DigitalOcean's terms effectively say, and it is the only safe default when a page refuses to state one.

## What we could not verify

We are not going to fill this table with guesses. Vultr, Linode, Contabo, and Liquid Web each refused an automated read of their policy text on 2026-10-09, so their cells say "not verifiable" rather than a number. That is a real result, not a gap in our research: **if a reader with a normal browser cannot confirm the term, the term is functionally unpublished.**

We also will not average these numbers into a single "industry standard refund window." An average across zero, 14, 30, and unknown would be a number no provider promises and no buyer can use.

## The one-line takeaway

Before you buy any VPS deal, find the refund sentence on the provider's own page and write down the day it expires. If you cannot find that sentence, the deal is carrying a cost you have not priced — and the providers that publish a number are, on this specific axis, the ones competing for your business.

articles.title: What "Renews at $X" Means on a VPS Deal Page
articles.description: A VPS deal's discount badge never equals your renewal increase. Here is the one-line formula, tested against eight real plan cards, to get next year's price before you buy.
articles.question: When a VPS deal page says "renews at $X", what will I actually pay next year, and how do I calculate it before I buy?
articles.body:
“Renews at $X” means the price on the card is introductory and your next term bills at $X. On the eight VPS plan cards we read on two official provider pages today, renewal cost between **11% and 72% more** than the introductory payments for the same length of service — and in all eight cases the increase was *larger* than the discount percentage printed on the badge. That is not accidental. It is arithmetic, and it runs in one direction only.

## The one-line answer: your renewal increase is bigger than the discount

If a card advertises a discount of **d** (as a fraction, so 42% off means d = 0.42), and renewal happens at the undiscounted rate:

```
renewal increase = d / (1 - d)

year-two price = year-one price x 1/(1 - d)
```

The reason is simple. The introductory rate is the list rate minus the discount: `intro = list x (1 - d)`. Renewal goes back to the list rate. So `renewal / intro = 1/(1 - d)`, and the increase is `d/(1 - d)`.

A 50% off badge is therefore not “half price, then a bit more”. It is **+100%** — year two costs twice year one. Nobody prints that sentence on the card.

## Eight plan cards, two vendors, one pattern

We read two official VPS pages on 2026-10-08 and applied the formula to every card that printed a renewal figure.

**Namecheap VPS plans** — each card prints both numbers in one sentence, in the form *“You pay $X — renews at $Y/year”*:

- **Spark** — pay $46.56, renews at $58.56/year. Real increase **+25.8%**. Badge said 20% off → formula predicts +25%.
- **Pulsar** — pay $82.56, renews at $106.56/year. Real increase **+29.1%**. Badge said 23% off → formula predicts +30%.
- **Quasar** — pay $154.56, renews at $190.56/year. Real increase **+23.3%**. Badge said 19% off → formula predicts +23%.
- **Magnetar** — pay $298.56, renews at $346.56/year. Real increase **+16.1%**. Badge said 14% off → formula predicts +16%.
- **Hypernova** — pay $562.56, renews at $634.56/year. Real increase **+12.8%**. Badge said 11% off → formula predicts +12%.

**Liquid Web VPS packages** — each card prints *“Introductory price. Renews at $X /year after the initial 1-year term.”*:

- **8 GB** — $150.30/mo (year one = $1,803.60), renews at **$2,004/year**. Real increase **+11.1%**. Badge said 10% off → formula predicts +11%.
- **16 GB** — $175.50/mo (year one = $2,106.00), renews at **$2,676/year**. Real increase **+27.1%**. Badge said 21% off → formula predicts +27%.
- **32 GB** — $256.50/mo (year one = $3,078.00), renews at **$5,280/year**. Real increase **+71.5%**. Badge said 42% off → formula predicts +72%.

Eight out of eight. On seven of them the formula lands within about one percentage point of the printed numbers; the widest gap is Pulsar (+30% predicted vs +29.1% actual), because the badge percentage itself is rounded. Read the [Namecheap VPS plans](https://www.namecheap.com/hosting/vps/) and the [Liquid Web VPS packages](https://www.liquidweb.com/vps-hosting/packages/) pages yourself and run the division — the arithmetic is visible on the page.

## Why the badge understates it

Two things do the work.

**Different denominators.** The badge measures the discount against the *undiscounted monthly rate*. Your increase is measured against *what you actually paid*. Those are different bases, so the two percentages can never be equal — the increase is always the larger one.

**Different units.** Liquid Web's cards put the promo per month and the renewal per year: “$150.30/mo” against “$2,004/year”. Converted to one unit, that is $150.30/mo now versus $167.00/mo after renewal. Namecheap's cards are easier to read because both figures land in the same sentence and the same unit.

So when you see a monthly promo next to an annual renewal, convert before you compare. That single step is the whole trick.

## The conversion table you can copy

Badge → the increase you actually get at renewal, assuming renewal occurs at the undiscounted rate (which is exactly what all eight cards above state):

```
10% off  ->   +11%
20% off  ->   +25%
25% off  ->   +33%
30% off  ->   +43%
40% off  ->   +67%
42% off  ->   +72%
50% off  ->  +100%
60% off  ->  +150%
65% off  ->  +186%
67% off  ->  +203%
70% off  ->  +233%
```

Read it backwards as well: a “70% off” VPS deal, stated honestly, is “year two costs about 3.3× year one”. Both sentences describe the same offer. Only one of them appears on the card.

## Read the verb, not just the number

The wording around the figure carries its own meaning:

- **“renews at $X”** — an exact figure. Used on both the Namecheap and Liquid Web cards above. This is the most useful field on a VPS page.
- **“renews from $X”** — a floor, not a promise. The actual renewal can be higher. Namecheap uses this form on its promotional tiles for other products.
- **“renews for $X”** — exact, equivalent to “at”.
- **“Was $X/mo”** — the undiscounted monthly rate. Handy shortcut: the renewal monthly rate is close to this number. On Namecheap's cards, “was $4.88/mo” matches the $58.56/year renewal exactly ($4.88 × 12).
- **“upon renewal $X”** — the phrasing review sites and community deal posts use. It is their summary of the vendor's terms, not the vendor's own wording. Verify it on the vendor's page.
- **“after the initial N-year term”** — gives you the jump date. A 2-year initial term moves the increase to month 25, not month 13, which changes the answer if you only plan to keep the server 18 months.

## What today's scan could and could not verify

Our own scan run at **2026-10-08T01:06:57Z** attempted eight official pricing and promotion pages. Five returned readable content; the pricing pages for Vultr and Linode (Akamai) and three Contabo URLs did not, so this article prints **no renewal figure for them**. An unreadable official page is not a license to estimate one.

The Hostinger VPS page was readable, and a single scan returned **four separate discount entries from that one page: 70%, 67%, 65% and 63% off**. Two things follow.

First, four different discount percentages on one page tells you the percentage is a marketing field attached to particular plan and term combinations — not a property of the provider. Second, if those badges behaved like the eight verified cards above, they would imply year-two increases of roughly +233%, +203%, +186% and +170% respectively. **We did not capture Hostinger's renewal prices in this scan, so those four numbers are unknown, not confirmed.** Use them as the question to take to the checkout page, not as Hostinger's renewal price.

## The other model: no promo to jump from

Not every provider plays this game. Hetzner's billing FAQ describes servers with both a monthly price cap and an hourly rate, where the bill never exceeds the monthly cap, and where a server is billed for as long as it exists — including while powered off, because resources stay allocated to it. Prices move to current pricing on certain actions: rescaling a server, restoring a deleted one, or moving it to a project in a different currency.

On that model there is no renewal jump to compute. There is a different failure mode: paying for a server you stopped using. The check changes accordingly — find the event that ends billing (deletion), not a renewal date.

## A 60-second check before you pay

1. **Find the undiscounted rate on the same card** — “was”, “regular”, or the renewal line. If none is present, mark renewal *unknown*.
2. **Put both figures in the same unit and the same term** — both monthly, or both annual.
3. **Divide renewal by promo.** That is your real multiplier. The badge is not.
4. **Find the jump date** — the end of the initial term — and price the whole horizon you intend to keep the server, not one year.
5. **Confirm the same renewal figure appears at checkout.** If the plan card and the checkout disagree, the checkout number is the one you will be charged. Keep a screenshot of both.
6. **If no renewal figure exists anywhere, do not assume the promo continues.** “Unknown” is a legitimate answer, and it usually means the deal is priced for people who forget to cancel.

Worth knowing: [Namecheap documents how hosting package renewal timing works](https://www.namecheap.com/support/knowledgebase/article.aspx/10567/21/hosting-packages-life-cycle/) relative to the billing cycle, and [how to renew a hosting package](https://www.namecheap.com/support/knowledgebase/article.aspx/9164/22/how-to-renew-your-hosting-account/), including renewing before the renewal control appears. Renewal mechanics are provider-specific; never transfer one provider's rule to another.

## Bottom line

- Convert the badge before you trust it: **increase = d / (1 − d)**. A 42% off VPS deal is a +72% renewal, verified on the [Liquid Web packages page](https://www.liquidweb.com/vps-hosting/packages/).
- **“Renews at $X” is the most honest field on a VPS page.** When a card has it you can do the math in ten seconds; when it does not, you are guessing.
- **Compare on a 24- or 36-month horizon**, not month one. The ranking of two VPS deals frequently flips once renewal is included.
- **Prefer pages that print renewal.** Of the pages we checked today, both vendors that published a renewal figure did so on the plan card itself. That transparency is worth more than a slightly bigger headline discount.

The cheapest VPS deal is not the one with the biggest badge. It is the one whose year-two price you already know.

articles.title: Cheap VPS Deals and SLA Credits: What You Actually Get Paid When the Server Goes Down
articles.description: Read off providers' own pages on 2026-10-14: DigitalOcean's CPU Droplet SLA has exactly one tier — below 99.99% it pays 100% of the affected Droplet's monthly charge, and the trigger is about four minutes of downtime. Hetzner publishes 99.9% annual network availability with no credit at all, Hostinger's VPS terms say the uptime guarantee applies 'if any', and Namecheap bills $10.00 to bring a failed server back online.
articles.question: If my cheap VPS goes down, how much money do I actually get back, and how do I claim it?
articles.body:
**Read off the providers' own pages on 2026-10-14, the answer for the four VPS brands that dominate cheap deals is: DigitalOcean pays 100% of the affected Droplet's monthly charge the moment a single Droplet misses 99.99% in a month — a threshold of roughly four minutes — but you have to email `success@digitalocean.com` yourself within two billing cycles and the money arrives as non-refundable credit. Hetzner publishes 99.9% and pays nothing. Hostinger's VPS contract says the uptime guarantee applies "if any". Namecheap prints 99.9% on its plan table and charges $10.00 to restore a failed server.** The percentages you see in marketing are the easy part; the payout mechanism is where the four diverge completely.

## DigitalOcean's VPS SLA has one row, not a ladder

The [DigitalOcean CPU Droplet SLA](https://www.digitalocean.com/sla/cpu-droplets) (last updated June 3, 2025) commits to "a Monthly Uptime Percentage of 99.99% for each individual Droplet instance" and — this is the part nobody quotes — its service credit table contains exactly one line:

> less than 99.99% → 100%

That is the whole table. Not 10%, not 25%, not a sliding scale. Compare it with DigitalOcean's own other SLAs, read the same day: the [GPU Droplet SLA](https://www.digitalocean.com/sla/gpu-droplets) (last updated October 21, 2025) commits to only **99%** and pays 10% / 25% / 50% in three tiers, capping at 50%. The [DOKS SLA](https://www.digitalocean.com/sla/doks) commits to 99.95% and pays 10% / 25% / 100%. So the cheapest product has the tightest target *and* the most generous payout — and the one product where a breach is easiest to prove.

Two more structural points hide in the definitions. The credit applies **per Droplet**: "Service Credits apply only to charges incurred for the specific Droplet resources affected." And credits are "credited towards future invoices", are "non-refundable", and are issued "within one billing cycle" of verification.

## The trigger is about four minutes — and the payout is the same for five minutes as for thirty days

The SLA defines Monthly Uptime Percentage as `(Total minutes in the month - Minutes of Unavailability) / Total minutes in the month`. So the downtime you are allowed before the 99.99% line breaks is 0.01% of the month:

| Month length | Total minutes | Downtime allowed at 99.99% |
|---|---|---|
| 28 days (February, non-leap) | 40,320 | **4 min 1.9 s** |
| 29 days | 41,760 | **4 min 10.6 s** |
| 30 days | 43,200 | **4 min 19.2 s** |
| 31 days | 44,640 | **4 min 27.8 s** |
