Your allowance moves with the calendar — you get 25.9 seconds more downtime in a 31-month than in a February — but in every case it rounds to **four whole minutes**. Counted in whole minutes, the fifth minute of unavailability in a month is what flips you from $0 to 100%.

Because the payout is binary rather than proportional, the arithmetic gets strange. Take DigitalOcean's cheapest Basic Droplet, **$0.00595/hr and $4.00/mo** (512 MiB / 1 vCPU / 10 GiB / 500 GiB transfer, read from [the pricing page](https://www.digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets) today). Its proportional value per minute of downtime is $4.00 ÷ 43,200 = $0.0000926. Now compare what the SLA actually pays:

| Outage length in a 30-day month | Proportional value | What the SLA pays | Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 minutes (inside the allowance) | $0.00037 | **$0** | 0x |
| 5 minutes | $0.00046 | **$4.00** | 8,640x |
| 1 hour | $0.00556 | **$4.00** | 720x |
| 24 hours | $0.13333 | **$4.00** | 30x |
| Full month | $4.00 | **$4.00** | 1x |

The multiple is simply 43,200 ÷ minutes of downtime, capped at the month's charge. **A five-minute outage and a thirty-day outage pay the identical $4.00.** There is no incentive in the contract for DigitalOcean to restore you quickly once the line has been crossed, and no extra compensation for you if it doesn't.

## The "100%" is 100% of one Droplet, not of your bill

Because the SLA "applies separately to each Droplet you use", the percentage you recover depends on how much of your fleet broke. Take ten 1 GiB Basic Droplets at $6.00/mo each — a $60.00/mo fleet:

| Incident | Machine-minutes lost | Credit | Share of the $60 bill |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Droplet down the whole month | 43,200 | **$6.00** | 10.0% |
| 2 Droplets down the whole month | 86,400 | **$12.00** | 20.0% |
| All 10 Droplets down 3 minutes each | 30 | **$0.00** | 0% |
| 1 Droplet down 5 minutes | 5 | **$6.00** | 10.0% |
| All 10 Droplets down 5 minutes each | 50 | **$60.00** | 100% |

Read the third and fourth rows together. **Ten Droplets each losing three minutes costs you 30 machine-minutes and pays $0. One Droplet losing five minutes costs you 5 machine-minutes and pays $6.00.** The worse incident, by any operational measure, is the one that pays nothing. If your load balancer returns errors during those three-minute blips, your users saw an outage and your SLA saw a perfect month.

## How to file, and the deadline that differs per product

For CPU Droplets the SLA says: "To request a Service Credit, contact DigitalOcean at success @digitalocean .com within two (2) billing cycles of the month when the downtime occurred. Include the email address associated with your account, affected Droplet resource details, and outage dates/times."

That is an email address, not a form, not a ticket, and not an automatic adjustment. **Nothing happens unless you notice, document and write.** And the deadline is not the same across the products on the same account:

| DigitalOcean product | Uptime target | Credit shape | Deadline to claim | Extra conditions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU Droplets | 99.99% monthly | 100% of affected Droplet | **2 billing cycles**, by email | Non-refundable; toward future invoices |
| Volumes Block Storage | 99.99% monthly | "100% of lost time at the hourly rate incurred" | **3 months** | Unavailability = all requests fail for **more than 5 minutes** |
| DOKS (HA control plane) | 99.95% monthly | 10% / 25% / 100% | **3 months** | Worker nodes covered by the Droplet SLA instead |
| GPU Droplets | **99%** monthly | 10% / 25% / **50% max** | **Notify within 24 hours** or forfeit; claim within 3 months | Credits **expire after 90 days**; none issued if the amount is **≤ $1** |

The GPU row is worth staring at: 99% monthly means 1% of a 30-day month is allowed — 432 minutes, or **7 h 12 min**, which is 100x the CPU allowance — and yet you must give written notice within 24 hours of the downtime starting or you lose the claim entirely. On one account, a GPU Droplet claim can be time-barred in a day while a CPU Droplet claim has roughly two months.

Two clauses in the [DigitalOcean Terms of Service](https://www.digitalocean.com/legal/terms-of-service-agreement) sit above all four. §6.5: "all credits, whether previously offered or otherwise, are revocable or subject to early expiration at any time and for any reason or no reason by us." §8.3: "The Service Level Agreements do not apply to Beta Services." The credit you earned is discretionary, and it does not exist at all on anything labelled beta or preview.

Finally, what counts. "Unavailability" is defined as loss of connectivity over the Droplet's public, reserved or private IP **due to the failure of DigitalOcean infrastructure**, or loss of read/write access to the root disk. And the exclusion list removes scheduled maintenance, customer-initiated downtime, "issues arising from customer application code or configuration errors", account restrictions and force majeure. **A Droplet that is up but slow, or dropping half its packets, is not "unavailable" under this definition** — the word is *loss*, not degradation.

## What the other three actually publish

**Hetzner** — §3.3 of its [Terms and Conditions](https://www.hetzner.com/legal/terms-and-conditions/) reads: *"We undertake to make economically reasonable efforts to achieve an annual average network availability of 99.9% at our data centers."* Three things matter here. It is an **endeavour**, not a commitment. It is **annual**, so a single catastrophic month can be averaged away against eleven quiet ones. And it is **network availability at the data centres** — not your cloud server. Over a year, 0.1% of 525,600 minutes is **8 h 45 min 36 s** of permitted downtime against DigitalOcean's 0.01% monthly, which works out to 52 min 34 s per year — exactly 10x tighter. Hetzner's T&C contains no service credit table at all.

**Hostinger** — §5 of the [Universal Terms of Service Agreement](https://www.hostinger.com/legal/universal-terms-of-service-agreement) that governs its VPS plans says: *"The service uptime guarantee applicable to specific Services, if any, is defined in other documents (e.g., specific Service agreement)... You acknowledge and agree that we assume no liability to you or any other party with regard thereto."* The contract you click through contains **no uptime number**. The guarantee is contingent — "if any" — and any liability is disclaimed in the same sentence.

**Namecheap** — its [VPS page](https://www.namecheap.com/hosting/vps/) does print a number: the spec table lists **Uptime 99.9%** for all five plans, glossed as "the monthly measurement of your server's accessibility to the Internet". At 99.9% monthly, a 30-day month permits 43 min 12 s of downtime. The page publishes no credit mechanism, no claim process and no SLA link. What it does publish is a price pointing the other way: under Complete management, *"Restore server failure — If the server fails, our Tech Support will bring the server back online"* is listed at **$10.00 flat rate per restore**, with *"Fix server failure cause"* at **$10.00 per hour**. On a Spark plan billed at **$46.56/year**, one restore is **21.5%** of a year's hosting cost. The only published money remedy on the page is a 30-day money-back guarantee, which expires 30 days after purchase and never applies to month nine.

**Liquid Web** — its [WordPress VPS page](https://www.liquidweb.com/wordpress-hosting/vps-wordpress/) carries the boldest number of the four: *"Uptime SLA — We guarantee your network and power are available 100% of the time."* Read the scope: **network and power**, not your VPS, not your database, not your application. No credit, no claim process and no remedy appears anywhere on that page or on the VPS packages page (which today shows an 8 GB plan at $150.30/mo with "10% OFF", and up to 42%/45% off for 1- and 2-year terms, and mentions uptime nowhere).

## What we could not verify today, and why we did not fill it in

We do not bypass bot protection and we do not estimate unreadable numbers, so these are stated as unread rather than guessed:

- **Vultr** — `vultr.com/legal/sla/` returned 403 to a direct request. No SLA read.
- **Namecheap legal** — `namecheap.com/legal/hosting/service-level-agreement/` returned 403. The 99.9% above comes from its public VPS plan table only; we could not read a credit clause.
- **Liquid Web legal** — both `liquidweb.com/legal/service-level-agreement/` and `liquidweb.com/about/legal/service-level-agreement/` returned 403. The 100% statement above is marketing copy from a product page, not the SLA document.
- **Hetzner SLA** — `hetzner.com/legal/service-level-agreement/` returns a legal-notice shell with no SLA text. The 99.9% figure above is from the general T&C, §3.3.
- **Hostinger** — `hostinger.com/legal/service-level-agreement` returned 404. There is no public SLA page to read; §5 of the universal terms is the only uptime language we could reach.
- **DigitalOcean** — `docs.digitalocean.com/support/how-do-i-request-an-sla-credit/` returned 404. There is no support article for the claim process; the `/sla/cpu-droplets` page is the only source, and note that `digitalocean.com/sla` is an index of **14 separate SLAs** — there is no single "DigitalOcean SLA" to point at.

## What to do, in order

1. **Instrument before you need it.** Every credit mechanism above is claim-driven. If you cannot produce dates and times per affected resource, you have nothing to send. A 1-minute-interval external ping to each VPS costs nothing and is the entire difference between $0 and 100%.
2. **Know your trigger.** On DigitalOcean CPU Droplets it is the fifth minute of unavailability in a calendar month. On Volumes it is five minutes of *complete* request failure. On Hetzner and Hostinger there is no trigger, because there is no payout.
3. **File inside the shortest deadline you have.** Two billing cycles for CPU Droplets; three months for Volumes and DOKS; **24 hours** for GPU Droplets. Put the deadline in your calendar the day an incident ends, not the day you get around to it.
4. **Calculate the claim before you send it.** Credit = (monthly charge of the affected Droplets only) × (credit tier). On a ten-node fleet with one node down, expect 10% of the bill, not 100%.
5. **Treat credits as store credit, not compensation.** DigitalOcean's are non-refundable and future-only, revocable under §6.5, and GPU credits expire in 90 days. Budget as if the payout were zero and the SLA is a signal about reliability, not an insurance policy.
6. **When comparing VPS deals, compare the mechanism, not the number.** 99.99% monthly with a binary 100% payout (DigitalOcean) and 99.9% annual with no payout (Hetzner) are not two similar products with slightly different decimals. They are, respectively, a claim you can file for $4.00 and a claim you cannot file at all.

articles.title: Who Actually Collects the VAT on Your VPS Deal
articles.description: Nobody on a VPS deal page tells you who charges the tax. Read the hosts' own billing docs side by side and one rule governs all of them — the collector is set by your tax location, and that location is seeded from the billing address on the payment method you attach first.
articles.question: On a VPS deal, who collects the VAT — the host, the payment provider, or me — and what actually decides it?
articles.body:
Four parties can end up accounting for the VAT on a VPS deal, and which one you get is decided before you ever see a price with tax on it: **the host**, **the marketplace vendor**, **you**, or **nobody at all**. Every tax document we read on 2026-10-09 keys that decision to a single variable — your tax location — and every one of them derives that location from an address attached to your payment method. DigitalOcean states it plainly: *"Your tax location is typically based on your account address, which is initially set to the payment address of your primary payment method when you sign up."* Hostinger goes further and puts the country dropdown **on the payment step itself**: *"Once you have chosen a period and created your account, you will be asked to select a payment method. Before submitting the payment, select your country."*

So the payment rail is not what matters — the address on the rail is. That distinction is worth real money: on DigitalOcean's own published schedule, the identical $6.00/mo Basic Droplet invoices at **$6.30 in the UAE and $7.62 in Hungary**, a 21% spread on the same resource, with no VPN, no coupon and no plan change.

## The four collectors, and how to tell which one you got

| Collector | When it applies | Documented example |
|---|---|---|
| **The host** | Your tax location appears on the host's published country schedule and you have no valid business tax ID on file | DigitalOcean charges EU VAT at the member-state rate; Hetzner charges Germany 19% |
| **The marketplace vendor** | You buy through a marketplace and your location is one where the platform has pushed collection to the seller | DigitalOcean Marketplace: Japan (JCT), Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and the UAE are all **"Vendor"**, not DigitalOcean |
| **You** | You are a registered business in a reverse-charge or withholding regime | Hetzner: EU customers with a valid VAT ID are invoiced *"according to the 'Reverse-Charge' procedure, without German tax"*; Tanzania: *"you may be required to withhold 15% of the gross payment"* |
| **Nobody** | Your location is outside every schedule the host publishes | Hetzner: *"Customers from these countries will receive their invoice without VAT"* |

The second row is the one nobody writes about. DigitalOcean publishes an explicit Responsibility to Collect and Remit Taxes matrix for its Marketplace, and for **four of the twenty jurisdictions listed — Japan, Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and the UAE — the answer is "Vendor," not DigitalOcean**, for both domestic and cross-border sales. If you buy a VPS-adjacent service through that marketplace in Zurich, the company whose logo is on the invoice is not the company doing the remitting.

The third row is where the money actually hides. Tanzania is the clearest published case: DigitalOcean charges **18% VAT** *and separately*, under the Tanzania Income Tax Act, a registered Tanzanian business *"may be required to withhold 15% of the gross payment for digital services from DigitalOcean."* The doc is explicit that *"Withholding tax is separate from value-added tax."* One purchase, two tax mechanisms, two different remitters.

## What a $6.00 VPS actually invoices at, by tax location

DigitalOcean's published schedule lists **39 tax locations** with rates from 5% to 27%. Applying those rates to the $6.00/mo Basic 1 GiB Droplet list price:

| Tax location | Published rate | Landed monthly on $6.00 |
|---|---|---|
| United Arab Emirates | 5% | **$6.30** |
| Thailand | 7% | $6.42 |
| Switzerland | 8.1% | $6.49 |
| Singapore | 9% | $6.54 |
| Australia / Japan / South Korea / Vietnam | 10% | $6.60 |
| India / Peru / Tanzania / Uganda | 18% | $7.08 |
| Germany (EU) | 19% | $7.14 |
| United Kingdom | 20% | $7.20 |
| Russia | 22% | $7.32 |
| Iceland | 24% | $7.44 |
| Norway | 25% | $7.50 |
| Finland (EU) | 25.5% | $7.53 |
| Hungary (EU) | 27% | **$7.62** |

DigitalOcean notes that *"Prices listed on the DigitalOcean website do not include applicable VAT charges"* — so every figure in the right-hand column is a number the pricing page will never show you.

Now the part that deletes the top of that table entirely: *"If you have a valid VAT ID in the European Union, you can add it to your team to remove tax charges from your invoice. If you have a valid VAT ID but don't add it to your team, your invoice includes tax charges."* The 27% is not a fact about Hungary. It is a fact about whether you typed a number into a form.

## Two hosts, same day, three different EU rates

We read DigitalOcean's EU VAT table and Hetzner's VAT page on the same day. They disagree on three member states:

| EU country | DigitalOcean | Hetzner |
|---|---|---|
| Estonia | 24% | 22% |
| Luxembourg | 16% | 17% |
| Romania | 21% | 19% |

They also disagree on South Africa: DigitalOcean publishes **15.5%** (effective 1 May 2019), Hetzner publishes **15.00%** (effective 1 January 2021). Hetzner's table carries "Starting on" dates; DigitalOcean's does not. We are not going to adjudicate which is current — the point for a buyer is that the rate on your invoice is whatever the host's billing engine decided, and two major hosts reading the same statute land on different numbers. Check the invoice, not the schedule.

Hetzner also splits the world differently from DigitalOcean. Where DigitalOcean applies one EU regime, Hetzner has five outcomes: **Germany 19%**, **EU with a valid VAT ID → reverse charge, no German tax**, **EU without one → the VAT rate of your country of origin**, **a short list of non-EU countries** (Australia 10%, Norway 25%, Singapore 9%, South Africa 15%, Switzerland 8.10%, UK 20%, plus sales tax in Texas, Utah, Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico), and **everyone else → no VAT**. Hetzner is also the only one of the two that charges US state sales tax by name: *"We charge an 8% sales tax for customers in Texas... We use the address in your account to figure this out."*

## The Hostinger trap: the VAT you paid is gone

Hostinger's tax page contains a sentence that should be printed on every checkout screen: *"Due to taxes being forwarded automatically, the VAT already applied to an invoice cannot be refunded."* And *"Invoices already issued will remain unchanged."*

The consequence is procedural, not theoretical. The VAT ID field lives on the payment step — *"Before submitting the payment, select your country"* — and if you skip it, Hostinger's only remedy is prospective: *"If you didn't add your tax identification code during the purchasing process... The new information will appear on your future invoices. Invoices already issued will remain unchanged."* Buying a 24-month promotional term and remembering your VAT number in month two costs you the tax on month one permanently.

There is also a ceiling on what Hostinger will even issue. Tax-compliant invoices are available **only** for entities with a valid tax ID in the EU/Northern Ireland, India or Indonesia; *"tax invoices cannot be issued for countries outside the EU/Northern Ireland, India, and Indonesia."* A UAE-registered company *"receive[s] a regular invoice showing VAT charged, rather than a fiscal invoice"* — and Hostinger charges UAE companies **5%**. If your finance team needs a reclaimable fiscal invoice, that is a purchasing decision you make before the order, not after.

## What the deal pages tell you: nothing

We opened the three biggest sites ranking for VPS deals. LowEndBox lists a German VPS at "€3.49/Month" and a Dutch one in euros with **no tax qualifier anywhere on the page** — despite both being in VAT-applicable jurisdictions. Liquid Web's VPS packages page shows three cards at $150.30, $175.50 and $256.50/mo with renewal terms, and its closest thing to tax language is a value prop reading *"Clear inclusions and predictable pricing from day one"* — no tax, no VAT, no statement of whether those figures are inclusive or exclusive. Namecheap's public billing knowledgebase, checked the same day, publishes **no VAT or tax schedule at all**; its checkout is the only place the number appears.

A shopper cannot determine from any of those first screens what they will actually be charged. That is the gap, and it is identical across all three.

## The ten-second check before you buy

```
1. Identify your tax location  -> the billing address of the payment method
                                  you attach FIRST, not your nationality
2. Look up that location on the host's published tax schedule
   - listed?       -> host collects.  landed = posted x (1 + rate)
   - not listed?   -> host collects nothing.  Check whether YOUR country
                      requires you to self-account (reverse charge / WHT)
3. Buying on a marketplace?    -> check the "who remits" matrix.  In Japan,
                                  Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and the UAE on
                                  DigitalOcean Marketplace it is the VENDOR
4. Registered business?        -> enter the VAT/GST ID BEFORE you submit
                                  payment.  Already-paid VAT is not refundable
                                  at Hostinger, and prior invoices do not change
5. Compare landed prices, not posted prices
```

Step 4 is where the money is, and it is the one step every checkout flow lets you skip. The rate is not the decision — the form field is.

## What we could not verify

Vultr, Linode (Akamai) and Contabo pricing pages refused automated reads on 2026-10-09, and we did not reach their tax documentation, so no landed-cost figures for them appear here. Namecheap publishes no tax schedule in its public knowledgebase, so we cannot state what it charges or where — we can only state that the number is not published in the place a buyer would look. DigitalOcean lists Canada, the EU and the United States as "Varies" rather than as single rates; we have not resolved those to a per-jurisdiction number and have left them out of the table rather than estimating.

articles.description: Read off five hosts' own pages on 2026-10-19: not one of them will move your VPS to another region. articles.question: I bought a cheap VPS in the wrong datacenter — can I move it to another region, or do I have to rebuild from scratch?
articles.body:
**Read off five hosts' own pages on 2026-10-19: not one of them will move your VPS to another datacenter. Not one.** Three of the five publish an actual answer, and the three answers are shaped differently enough that the differences — not the price, not the RAM — decide what a wrong-region mistake costs you.

Hetzner states it in one line: *"It is not possible to change the location of an existing server."* DigitalOcean never says "no"; it says *"take a snapshot of your Droplet and then create new Droplet from the snapshot in the new datacenter"* — a rebuild, not a move. Hostinger is the only one of the three that gives you a real button: its KB explains that *"although the location of your Virtual Private Server (VPS) cannot be changed directly, you can reinstall it in a new location as an alternative"* — and then warns, in bold, that doing so *"will permanently delete all existing data, including backups and snapshots."*

So the answer to "can I move it" is **no, everywhere** — and the answer that actually matters is **what the substitute destroys on the way.** That is what this page measures.

## The one-line answer, per host (read 2026-10-19)

| Host | Can an existing VPS be moved to another region? | What the official path is | What survives | What dies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DigitalOcean** | No — rebuild | Snapshot → add image to the new region → create a new Droplet from it | Disk contents, user accounts, SSH keys | IPv4 address, backups, volume snapshots |
| **Hetzner** | No — *"not possible"* | Create a **new** server in the desired location from a Snapshot or Backup of the old one | Disk contents up to the moment of the snapshot | Anything written after the snapshot; the old server stays |
| **Hostinger** | No — reinstall in place | VPS → Plan details → **Change** → pick location → Next | Nothing | *"all existing data, including backups and snapshots"* |
| **Namecheap** | No published answer | None found | — | — |
| **Liquid Web** | No published answer | "Expert-led migrations" (marketing copy, no relocation policy) | — | — |

## DigitalOcean: the move is free, the snapshot is not

DigitalOcean's migration doc is unusually explicit about the sequence, and its pricing page is unusually explicit about the price. Put the two together and the cost of a region change on DigitalOcean is **$0.00 for the transfer and a per-GB monthly rent on the copy.**

From the snapshots pricing page: *"Snapshots are charged at $0.06 per GB per month for Droplets... There is a minimum charge of $0.01... There is no additional charge for making a snapshot available in multiple regions."* And from the how-to: *"By default, a Droplet snapshot is only available in the region where it was created. If you want to use a snapshot to create Droplets in other regions, you need to add the snapshot to those regions first."*

That means the geographic part of the move is free and the *storage* part keeps billing. Here is that rent worked out against every Basic (shared-CPU) tier on the pricing page, read 2026-10-19, using the full boot-disk size as the upper bound:

| Plan (slug) | vCPU / RAM | Boot disk | Price/mo | Snapshot rent/mo (disk × $0.06) | Rent as % of the plan | 24 h running both |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `s-1vcpu-512mb-10gb` | 1 / 0.5 GB | 10 GiB | $4.00 | $0.60 | **15.0%** | $0.14 |
| `s-1vcpu-1gb` | 1 / 1 GB | 25 GiB | $6.00 | $1.50 | **25.0%** | $0.21 |
| `s-1vcpu-2gb` | 1 / 2 GB | 50 GiB | $12.00 | $3.00 | **25.0%** | $0.43 |
| `s-2vcpu-2gb` | 2 / 2 GB | 60 GiB | $18.00 | $3.60 | **20.0%** | $0.64 |
| `s-2vcpu-4gb` | 2 / 4 GB | 80 GiB | $24.00 | $4.80 | **20.0%** | $0.86 |
| `s-4vcpu-8gb` | 4 / 8 GB | 160 GiB | $48.00 | $9.60 | **20.0%** | $1.71 |
| `s-8vcpu-16gb` | 8 / 16 GB | 320 GiB | $96.00 | $19.20 | **20.0%** | $3.43 |

Three things fall out of that table.

**The overlap is cheap; the snapshot is not.** Running old and new side by side for a day costs $0.14–$3.43 depending on tier. Leaving the snapshot behind costs 15%–25% of the machine's own price *every month*, indefinitely. On the 320 GiB tier, one year of a forgotten snapshot is **$230.40 — which is 57.6 months of the $4.00/mo Droplet**, i.e. 4.8 years of the cheapest machine on the platform, spent on a disk image.

**You cannot make the billing stop by moving the data off.** DigitalOcean's own support page: *"You cannot currently download DigitalOcean backups or snapshots, but you can use third-party tools to save your data locally."* The only lever that zeroes the $0.06/GB is deleting the snapshot — which deletes the copy. Hostinger's official instruction is the exact opposite: download first, *then* press the button.

**Time scales on used space, cost scales on disk.** *"Creating a backup or snapshot takes about 1 to 3 minutes per GB of used disk space"* — while the downsize doc notes that *"the entire disk is imaged, not only the data present on the disk."* A 320 GiB machine with 40 GB used snapshots in 40–120 minutes but is billed on the image. Budget the wall clock on used data; budget the invoice on the disk.

## The datacenter trap nobody warns you about

DigitalOcean's Droplet availability page (last updated 2026-08-25) lists **16 datacenters**: NYC1, NYC2, NYC3, AMS3, SFO2, SFO3, SGP1, LON1, FRA1, TOR1, BLR1, SYD1, ATL1, RIC1, MKC1, MEM1. They are not interchangeable.

- The classic plan families (Basic, General Purpose, CPU-Optimized, Memory-Optimized, Storage-Optimized) are **fully available in 11** of them, partially available in 4 (SFO2 *"Premium AMD CPUs are not available"*; ATL1, RIC1, MKC1 *"Only Premium … CPUs are available"*), and **not available at all in MEM1**.
- **v5 configurations are available in exactly 4** — ATL1, RIC1, MKC1, MEM1.

The overlap between those two sets is **zero**. There is not one datacenter where a v5 Droplet and a fully-provisioned classic Basic Droplet both exist. If you are on a v5 plan and you want to be in New York, Amsterdam or Singapore, the migration is not geographic — you are changing plan family at the same time, and the snapshot route will not carry the plan with it.

## The ratchet: a move is one-way on disk size

*"You cannot downsize a Droplet from a snapshot. Data is not always stored sequentially in memory, so reducing the size of a disk can result in data loss or corruption."* And the reason is structural: *"When creating a snapshot, the entire disk is imaged, not only the data present on the disk. This means that you can only create Droplets with as much disk space as the Droplet the snapshot was taken from, or more."*

So every snapshot-based region change has a floor: **the new machine's disk is ≥ the old machine's disk.** If part of why you wanted to move was to land somewhere cheaper and smaller, the official path cannot do it. DigitalOcean's own workaround is to *"create a smaller Droplet and then transfer your data over the new Droplet using `rsync`"* — a second migration method, on top of the snapshot one.

Two more casualties on the same page, both official:

- **Your IPv4 dies.** *"Unfortunately, you cannot preserve a Droplet's IP address when transferring the Droplet between regions, nor can you reassign a non-reserved IP address to another Droplet."* And you cannot pre-empt it: *"You cannot convert a Droplet IP address into a Reserved IP."* A Reserved IP is region-bound too, so it is a way to keep an address across *rebuilds in one region*, not across regions.
- **Volume snapshots do not move.** *"You cannot transfer volume snapshots to other regions."* Only Droplet snapshots can be added to another region.

## Hostinger: the only one-click move — and it deletes the safety net

Hostinger's KB article *"How to transfer your VPS to a different location in Hostinger"* (updated ~2 months before 2026-10-19) is the single most useful relocation document in this comparison, because it is the only one describing a button you press inside your existing plan:

> *"Although the location of your Virtual Private Server (VPS) cannot be changed directly, you can reinstall it in a new location as an alternative."*
> *"Important: Reinstalling your VPS in a new location will permanently delete all existing data, including backups and snapshots. To avoid losing important information, ensure you create and download a full backup via SFTP before proceeding."*

The steps are: VPS section → select the server → **VPS Plan details → Change** → choose the location from the dropdown → Next.

The collision with Hostinger's own product page is worth stating plainly. The VPS page (read the same day) lists **"Free weekly backups"** as an included feature on every plan — and the relocation procedure destroys backups and snapshots by design. So on Hostinger the host's own safety net is *inside the blast radius of the move*, and the only sanctioned way out is to pull 50–400 GB down over SFTP yourself first — the plan sizes on that page being KVM 1 (50 GB NVMe), KVM 2 (100 GB), KVM 4 (200 GB), KVM 8 (400 GB).

That gives you the cleanest rule in this whole comparison: **the easier the move, the more it deletes.** Hostinger's one-button move costs you every copy the host was holding for you. DigitalOcean's manual rebuild is slower, but the old Droplet keeps running while you test the new one, and the docs even recommend it — *"it can be worth the cost to retain the original Droplet and snapshots, run automated and manual tests."*

## Hetzner: flat no, plus a copy you must keep current

Hetzner's Cloud FAQ answers the question directly under the heading *"How can I change the location of my server?"*:

> *"It is not possible to change the location of an existing server. When you create a new server in the desired location, you can, however, choose to use a Snapshot or Backup of the existing server. The new server will then be a direct copy of the existing server."*

Two limits govern what you can copy, both from the backups/snapshots overview: **up to 7 Backup slots per server**, and **by default up to 30 Snapshots across all projects**. Snapshots also *"are never deleted or updated automatically"* — so unlike a rolling backup window, a Hetzner snapshot is a manual commitment.

And the caveat that decides whether a Hetzner move loses data: *"Make sure that your Snapshot is up to date. Changes that have been made on the server after the Snapshot was created, are not included in the Snapshot."* If your latest Backup is stale, the doc tells you to *"create a new Backup manually"* first. There is no automatic "sync the delta at cutover" step on any of the three hosts — the copy is as old as the copy.

Hetzner's IP economics are at least published, unlike the relocation itself: a Primary IPv4 is **€0.50 / $0.60 per month (€0.0008 / h)**, Primary IPv6 is free, each server holds one of each, and the account total is *"server limit multiplied by 2."* Hetzner's docs do not state whether a Primary IP can follow a server across locations, so treat your address as lost on a Hetzner move too.

## What the three comparison sites actually answer

Checked all three on 2026-10-19, first screen down:

- **LowEndBox** — the homepage's whole location system is a **filter taxonomy** (North America → West Coast / Inland / East Coast; Europe; Asia/Pacific — down to city), and the intro says *"Browse budget-friendly VPS and dedicated server offers by location, virtualization type, and special features like NVMe or DDoS protection."* Location is a shopping filter, not a lifecycle question. Nothing on the page says what happens after you buy.
- **Namecheap** — the VPS card on the homepage carries a price and a term and no location field at all. The nearest thing to a location control anywhere on that first screen is a URL parameter on the *shared hosting* buy link (`addons=server-location;server-location-us`).
- **Liquid Web** — the packages page never states when or how a datacenter is chosen. The only location text is *"With data centers in the U.S., Europe, and Australia"*, and the only migration text is the value-prop *"Our team has migrated thousands of sites. You choose the timing, we handle the technical details."* No relocation policy, no downtime figure, no cost.

None of the three gives an answer. That is the gap this page fills.

## Not verifiable (2026-10-19, no proxies, no UA spoofing)

- **Namecheap** — no relocation path is published. Its VPS knowledge-base section (`/support/knowledgebase/subcategory/48/vps/`) listed **46 articles** when read today and **none** concerns changing a server's location or datacenter; the VPS product page `/hosting/vps/` returned **403** to a direct fetch.
- **Liquid Web** — `/vps-hosting/packages/` returned **403** to a direct fetch; the quotes above come from reading the public page text, and the relocation policy itself is not published there.
- **Vultr** — `/pricing/` and the instance-move doc both returned **403**.
- **Linode / Akamai** — `techdocs.akamai.com` returned a navigation shell only (3.7 MB of SPA chrome, no article body); no cross-region migration text could be read.
- **Hetzner snapshot pricing** — the docs defer to *"the respective info box at hetzner.com/cloud"*, which is client-rendered and returned no figures. No Hetzner price is asserted on this page.

## What to do, in order

1. **Decide whether you are moving regions or moving plan families.** On DigitalOcean, if you are on v5, any target outside ATL1 / RIC1 / MKC1 / MEM1 forces a plan change at the same time — check `docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/availability/` before you snapshot anything.
2. **Take the copy, then take it again.** Hetzner's rule is the general rule: only what existed at snapshot time travels. On a busy server, quiesce the writers, snapshot, and verify.
3. **Budget the wall clock on used data and the invoice on disk.** 1–3 minutes per GB *used*; $0.06 per GB of *disk* per month, thereafter, forever.
4. **On DigitalOcean, put a calendar reminder on the snapshot.** At 15%–25% of the tier's monthly price, a snapshot nobody deleted is the most expensive thing most people leave behind after a move — and you cannot download it to make the billing stop.
5. **On Hostinger, download before you press Change.** Everything goes, including the "free weekly backups" the product page sells you on. 50–400 GB over SFTP is the official price of that button.
6. **Assume the IP is gone.** DigitalOcean says it outright; neither Hetzner nor Hostinger documents an address that follows a server to a new location. Lower your DNS TTL *before* you start, not after.
7. **If you also wanted to shrink, do not use the snapshot.** It can only grow. Use `rsync` onto a freshly-created smaller machine, and keep both running until you have tested.
